optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: e^5 is about 1.5 x 10^2, obtained by halving the exponent (for example using half the energy difference, 12.5 kJ mol^-1). Misconception: only half of the 25 kJ mol^-1 barrier reduction should be used in the exponent.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 25000/(8.314 x 300) = 10, the value of the exponent itself. Misconception: the answer is Ea/RT, forgetting that this quantity must be exponentiated.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: e^-10 is about 4.5 x 10^-5, obtained by inverting the sign in the exponent. Misconception: lowering the activation energy decreases the rate (the sign of the energy difference is reversed).

subtopic: Kp from equilibrium partial pressures with a partial pressure found by difference
learningObjective: Construct a Kp expression with correct stoichiometric exponents and evaluate it after deducing a missing partial pressure from the total pressure.
stem:
Sulfur trioxide is produced by the equilibrium:

2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g)

In a vessel at constant temperature the total pressure at equilibrium is 0.70 atm. The partial pressure of SO2 is 0.10 atm and that of O2 is 0.20 atm; the remaining pressure is due to SO3. What is the value of Kp?
explanation: First find the SO3 partial pressure by difference: p(SO3) = 0.70 - 0.10 - 0.20 = 0.40 atm. The equilibrium expression, using the stoichiometric coefficients as exponents, is Kp = p(SO3)^2 / [p(SO2)^2 x p(O2)] = (0.40)^2 / [(0.10)^2 x 0.20] = 0.16 / (0.01 x 0.20) = 0.16 / 0.002 = 80 atm^-1.

optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: (0.70)^2 / [(0.10)^2 x 0.20] = 0.49 / 0.002 = 245, obtained by using the total pressure (0.70 atm) as the SO3 partial pressure. Misconception: the total pressure equals the partial pressure of the product rather than the sum of all partial pressures.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 1/80 = 0.0125, obtained by writing reactants over products. Misconception: the equilibrium expression places reactant terms in the numerator and product terms in the denominator.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.16 / (0.10 x 0.20) = 8, obtained by squaring SO3 but not SO2. Misconception: the coefficient of 2 is applied only to the product, not to the reactant SO2.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.40 / (0.10 x 0.20) = 20, obtained by ignoring all stoichiometric coefficients as exponents. Misconception: partial pressures enter the expression to the first power regardless of the balancing numbers.

subtopic: First-order integrated kinetics: constant fractional decrease over equal time intervals
learningObjective: Apply the property that a first-order reactant falls by the same multiplicative factor over equal time intervals to predict a later concentration.
stem: A reaction that is first order in reactant A is followed at constant temperature. The concentration of A falls from 0.60 mol L^-1 to 0.36 mol L^-1 during the first 40 s. What will the concentration of A be after a further 40 s (that is, at t = 80 s)?
explanation: For a first-order reaction the concentration is multiplied by the same constant factor during equal time intervals, because [A] = [A]0 e^(-kt). In the first 40 s the factor is 0.36/0.60 = 0.60. During the next 40 s the concentration is multiplied by 0.60 again: 0.36 x 0.60 = 0.216 mol L^-1.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 0.36 x 0.60 x 0.60 = 0.13 mol L^-1, obtained by applying the decay factor twice more instead of once. Misconception: two additional 40 s intervals have elapsed beyond the measured point rather than one.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: first-order decay multiplies [A] by the same factor each 40 s. The factor is 0.36/0.60 = 0.60, so after a further interval [A] = 0.36 x 0.60 = 0.216 mol L^-1.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 0.36/2 = 0.18 mol L^-1, obtained by treating the first 40 s as one half-life and halving. Misconception: the interval over which concentration fell from 0.60 to 0.36 is a half-life (it is not, since 0.36 is not half of 0.60).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.60/2 = 0.30 mol L^-1, obtained by treating the whole 80 s as a single half-life of the original concentration. Misconception: the total elapsed time corresponds to one halving of the starting concentration.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.36 - 0.24 = 0.12 mol L^-1, obtained by subtracting the same fixed amount (0.24 mol L^-1) lost in the first interval. Misconception: the reaction loses a constant amount per unit time (zero-order behaviour) rather than a constant fraction.

subtopic: Gibbs free energy: temperature crossover for spontaneity from enthalpy and entropy
learningObjective: Combine enthalpy and entropy changes in DeltaG = DeltaH - T DeltaS to determine the temperature range over which a reaction with both terms negative is spontaneous.
stem:
For the gas-phase association reaction

A(g) + B(g) <=> C(g)

the standard enthalpy change is DeltaH0 = -60.0 kJ mol^-1 and the standard entropy change is DeltaS0 = -150 J mol^-1 K^-1, both essentially independent of temperature. Which statement correctly describes the thermodynamic spontaneity of the forward reaction under standard conditions?
choices: The forward reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures.
The forward reaction is spontaneous at no temperature.
The forward reaction is spontaneous only below 298 K.
The forward reaction is spontaneous only above 400 K.
The forward reaction is spontaneous only below 400 K.
explanation: Spontaneity requires DeltaG0 = DeltaH0 - T DeltaS0 < 0. Substituting: DeltaG0 = -60000 - T(-150) = -60000 + 150T (in J mol^-1). This is negative when 150T < 60000, i.e. T < 400 K. Both terms are negative, so the exothermic enthalpy favours reaction while the entropy decrease opposes it; the enthalpy term wins at low temperature. The crossover is T = DeltaH0/DeltaS0 = 60000/150 = 400 K, and the forward reaction is spontaneous only below it.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: claims spontaneity at every temperature. Misconception: a negative (exothermic) DeltaH0 guarantees spontaneity, ignoring the unfavourable negative entropy term that dominates at high temperature.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: claims the reaction is never spontaneous. Misconception: a negative DeltaS0 forbids spontaneity at all temperatures, ignoring the favourable enthalpy term that dominates below 400 K.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: uses 298 K as the boundary. Misconception: the standard reference temperature of 298 K is the crossover temperature, rather than the value DeltaH0/DeltaS0 = 400 K calculated from the data.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: places spontaneity above the crossover. Misconception: raising the temperature always increases spontaneity, overlooking that with DeltaS0 negative the -T DeltaS0 term grows more positive as T rises, disfavouring reaction at high T.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: DeltaG0 = -60000 + 150T is negative for T < 400 K, so the forward reaction is spontaneous only below the crossover temperature 60000/150 = 400 K.

subtopic: van't Hoff equation: enthalpy of reaction from K at two temperatures
learningObjective: Apply the two-point van't Hoff equation to extract the standard reaction enthalpy from equilibrium constants measured at two temperatures, with correct sign interpretation.
stem:
The equilibrium constant Kp for a gas-phase reaction is found to be 1.0 at 300 K and 10.0 at 400 K. Assuming the standard enthalpy change of reaction is independent of temperature, what is its approximate value?

(R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1; ln 10 is approximately 2.303.)
explanation: The two-point van't Hoff equation is ln(K2/K1) = -(DeltaH0/R)(1/T2 - 1/T1), which rearranges to DeltaH0 = R ln(K2/K1) x [T1 T2/(T2 - T1)]. Substituting: DeltaH0 = 8.314 x ln(10) x [(300 x 400)/(400 - 300)] = 8.314 x 2.303 x (120000/100) = 8.314 x 2.303 x 1200, which is about +23000 J mol^-1 = +23 kJ mol^-1. The positive sign is expected: K increases with temperature, so by Le Chatelier the reaction is endothermic.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: DeltaH0 = R ln(K2/K1) x T1 T2/(T2 - T1) = 8.314 x 2.303 x 1200, which is about +23 kJ mol^-1, endothermic because K rises with temperature.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 8.314 x 2.303 x 100 is about 1.9 kJ mol^-1, obtained by using the temperature difference (100 K) in place of the term T1 T2/(T2 - T1) = 1200 K. Misconception: the temperature factor is simply the difference in temperatures, not the product divided by the difference.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 8.314 x 350 x 2.303 is about 6.7 kJ mol^-1, obtained by inserting a single average temperature of 350 K instead of the two-point temperature term. Misconception: the relation can be handled with one average temperature rather than the full T1 T2/(T2 - T1) factor.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 8.314 x 1 x 1200 is about 10 kJ mol^-1, obtained by using log10(10) = 1 in place of ln(10) = 2.303. Misconception: the van't Hoff equation uses base-10 logarithms, so the factor of 2.303 is omitted.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: the correct magnitude but with a negative sign, concluding the reaction is exothermic. Misconception: an equilibrium constant that increases with rising temperature indicates an exothermic reaction (the sign of the van't Hoff relation is reversed).

subtopic: Solution concentration: mixing electrolyte solutions and ion concentration
learningObjective: Calculate the concentration of a specific ion after mixing two electrolyte solutions, accounting for the stoichiometry of dissociation and additive volumes.
stem: A chemist prepares a solution by mixing 250 mL of 0.40 mol L⁻¹ sodium chloride (NaCl) with 150 mL of 0.20 mol L⁻¹ calcium chloride (CaCl₂). Assuming that the volumes are additive and that both salts dissociate completely, what is the concentration of chloride ions (Cl⁻) in the final mixture?
explanation: Count the moles of chloride supplied by each salt, remembering that CaCl₂ releases two Cl⁻ per formula unit. From NaCl: 0.250 L × 0.40 mol L⁻¹ = 0.100 mol Cl⁻. From CaCl₂: 0.150 L × 0.20 mol L⁻¹ = 0.030 mol CaCl₂, giving 2 × 0.030 = 0.060 mol Cl⁻. Total chloride = 0.100 + 0.060 = 0.160 mol. The total volume is 250 + 150 = 400 mL = 0.400 L, so [Cl⁻] = 0.160 mol / 0.400 L = 0.40 mol L⁻¹.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 0.80 mol L⁻¹ adds the chloride molarity contributed by each source before dilution (0.40 M from NaCl plus 0.20 × 2 = 0.40 M from CaCl₂). This ignores the mutual dilution that occurs when the two solutions are combined.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 0.30 mol L⁻¹ is the arithmetic mean of the two stated molarities (0.40 and 0.20). This treats concentration as if it could simply be averaged, ignoring both the differing volumes and the number of chloride ions per formula unit.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 0.33 mol L⁻¹ comes from counting only one Cl⁻ per CaCl₂ (0.100 + 0.030 = 0.130 mol over 0.400 L). It reflects the common oversight of not multiplying by the number of chloride ions released on dissociation.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.64 mol L⁻¹ divides the correct total chloride (0.160 mol) by only the 0.250 L of NaCl solution. It arises from forgetting that mixing dilutes the chloride into the combined 0.400 L volume.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: total Cl⁻ = 0.100 mol (from NaCl) + 0.060 mol (from CaCl₂, two Cl⁻ each) = 0.160 mol, divided by the additive volume of 0.400 L, giving 0.40 mol L⁻¹.

subtopic: Electrolysis: Faraday's laws and mass of metal deposited
learningObjective: Apply Faraday's laws of electrolysis to relate charge, the number of electrons transferred and the mass of metal deposited at an electrode.
stem: A constant current of 5.00 A is passed for exactly 1.00 hour through molten aluminium chloride, depositing aluminium at the cathode with 100% current efficiency. Given that the Faraday constant is 96 500 C mol⁻¹ and the relative atomic mass of aluminium is 27.0, what mass of aluminium is deposited?
explanation: First find the charge passed: Q = I × t = 5.00 A × (1.00 × 3600 s) = 18 000 C. Moles of electrons = Q / F = 18 000 / 96 500 = 0.1865 mol. The cathode reaction is Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al, so 3 mol of electrons are needed per mole of aluminium: moles Al = 0.1865 / 3 = 0.0622 mol. Mass = 0.0622 mol × 27.0 g mol⁻¹ = 1.68 g.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 0.028 g results from converting 1.00 hour to only 60 s (multiplying by 60 once instead of by 3600). Using Q = 300 C in an otherwise correct calculation gives this value, reflecting an error in the time-to-seconds conversion.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 5.04 g omits the division by the number of electrons entirely, treating the process as if one electron deposited one aluminium atom (Al⁺). This ignores the +3 charge of Al³⁺.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: Q = 18 000 C gives 0.1865 mol of electrons; dividing by 3 (because Al³⁺ needs three electrons) yields 0.0622 mol Al, which is 1.68 g.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 2.52 g comes from dividing the moles of electrons by 2 rather than 3, i.e. treating the ion as Al²⁺. It encodes an incorrect charge on the aluminium ion.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 15.1 g multiplies the moles of electrons by 3 instead of dividing by 3. It reverses the role of the electron stoichiometric coefficient in Faraday's law.

subtopic: Graham's law of effusion and molar mass determination
learningObjective: Use Graham's law of effusion to determine an unknown molar mass from relative effusion times, applying the inverse-square-root relationship correctly.
stem: Equal volumes of oxygen gas (O₂, relative molecular mass 32) and an unknown gas are allowed to effuse through the same small orifice under identical conditions of temperature and pressure. The oxygen takes 60 s to effuse completely, whereas the unknown gas takes 90 s. What is the relative molecular mass of the unknown gas?
explanation: By Graham's law, the rate of effusion is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass: rate ∝ 1/√M. For a fixed volume, effusion time is inversely proportional to rate, so time ∝ √M. Therefore t_unknown / t_O₂ = √(M_unknown / M_O₂). Rearranging: M_unknown = M_O₂ × (t_unknown / t_O₂)² = 32 × (90/60)² = 32 × 2.25 = 72.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: since time ∝ √M, M_unknown = 32 × (90/60)² = 32 × 2.25 = 72.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 39 ≈ 32 × √(90/60) takes the square root of the time ratio instead of squaring it. It inverts the exponent that should be applied to the time ratio.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 14 ≈ 32 × (60/90)² both inverts the time ratio and squares it. It combines the wrong direction of the ratio with the square-root/square confusion.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 48 = 32 × (90/60) applies a linear proportionality between molar mass and time (rate ∝ 1/M). It omits the square root inherent in Graham's law.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 21 ≈ 32 × (60/90) inverts the time ratio, implicitly assuming that the heavier gas effuses faster. It has the direction of the molar-mass–rate relationship backwards.

subtopic: Successive ionization energies and group identification
learningObjective: Interpret successive ionization energy data to deduce the number of valence electrons and hence identify the group and identity of an element.
stem: The first five successive ionization energies (in kJ mol⁻¹) of a period-3 element are 578, 1817, 2745, 11 580 and 14 840. On the basis of these data, identify the element.
explanation: Successive ionization energies rise gradually while electrons are removed from the outer (valence) shell, then jump sharply once a stable noble-gas core is broken into. Here the values 578, 1817, 2745 increase modestly, but there is a very large jump between the 3rd (2745) and 4th (11 580) ionization energies — more than a fourfold increase. This means three electrons are relatively easy to remove and the fourth requires breaking into an inner shell, so the element has three valence electrons and belongs to Group 13. A period-3 Group-13 element is aluminium.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: the sharp jump between the 3rd and 4th ionization energies shows three easily removed valence electrons, indicating Group 13; in period 3 this is aluminium.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: magnesium (Group 2) has two valence electrons, so its dramatic jump comes after the 2nd ionization energy. This choice locates the jump after only two electrons.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: silicon (Group 14) has four valence electrons, so its large jump would appear after the 4th ionization energy, not the 3rd. This choice places the jump one electron too late.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: phosphorus (Group 15) has five valence electrons and would show a smooth rise through all five listed values, with the jump coming later. It over-counts the valence electrons.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: sodium (Group 1) would show its large jump immediately after the 1st ionization energy. Choosing Na misreads the first sizeable increase (578 → 1817) as the core-breaking jump.

subtopic: Galvanic cells: Nernst equation and non-standard cell potential
learningObjective: Apply the Nernst equation to calculate a non-standard galvanic cell potential from ion concentrations, handling the reaction quotient and electron number correctly.
stem: A galvanic cell operates on the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), for which the standard cell potential is E° = +1.10 V at 25 °C. In a particular cell the concentrations are [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 mol L⁻¹ and [Zn²⁺] = 1.0 mol L⁻¹. Using the Nernst equation E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q, what is the cell potential under these conditions?
explanation: The reaction quotient uses only the aqueous species (solids are excluded): Q = [Zn²⁺] / [Cu²⁺] = 1.0 / 0.010 = 100, so log Q = 2. Two electrons are transferred, so n = 2. Applying the Nernst equation: E = 1.10 − (0.059/2)(2) = 1.10 − 0.059 = 1.04 V. Because the product ion (Zn²⁺) is more concentrated than the reactant ion (Cu²⁺), the cell potential is slightly below the standard value.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1.10 V is simply E°, obtained by neglecting the Nernst correction term altogether. It treats non-standard concentrations as if they had no effect on the cell potential.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 1.16 V results from a sign error, adding rather than subtracting the correction term (1.10 + 0.059). Equivalently it comes from inverting Q so that log Q is taken as −2.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 0.98 V comes from omitting the division by n (or setting n = 1), giving E = 1.10 − 0.059 × 2 = 0.98 V. It ignores that two electrons are transferred in this reaction.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 1.22 V combines the sign error with omission of the division by n, giving 1.10 + 0.059 × 2. It doubles an already wrongly-signed correction.

subtopic: Redox titration: permanganate–iron(II) solution stoichiometry
learningObjective: Perform redox-titration stoichiometry to determine an analyte concentration, integrating the balanced reaction ratio with solution-concentration calculations.
stem: A 25.0 mL sample of an acidified solution containing iron(II) ions is titrated with 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ potassium permanganate (KMnO₄). The purple colour just persists after 24.0 mL of the permanganate solution has been added. The reaction is: MnO₄⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H₂O. What is the concentration of Fe²⁺ in the original sample?
explanation: Moles of MnO₄⁻ delivered = 0.0200 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0240 L = 4.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol. The balanced equation shows 5 mol Fe²⁺ react per 1 mol MnO₄⁻, so moles Fe²⁺ = 5 × 4.80 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.40 × 10⁻³ mol. This iron came from the 25.0 mL sample, so [Fe²⁺] = 2.40 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.0250 L = 0.096 mol L⁻¹.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: moles MnO₄⁻ = 4.80 × 10⁻⁴; × 5 gives 2.40 × 10⁻³ mol Fe²⁺; divided by 0.0250 L gives 0.096 mol L⁻¹.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 0.0192 mol L⁻¹ uses a 1:1 mole ratio between permanganate and iron(II), dividing 4.80 × 10⁻⁴ mol by 0.0250 L. It ignores the stoichiometric factor of 5 in the balanced equation.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 0.0038 mol L⁻¹ divides the permanganate moles by 5 instead of multiplying, giving 9.6 × 10⁻⁵ mol over 0.0250 L. It inverts the direction of the 5:1 stoichiometric ratio.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.100 mol L⁻¹ divides the correct moles of Fe²⁺ (2.40 × 10⁻³) by the titrant volume (24.0 mL) instead of the sample volume. It uses the wrong volume in the final concentration step.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.049 mol L⁻¹ divides the moles of Fe²⁺ by the combined volume of the two solutions (25.0 + 24.0 = 49.0 mL). Titration concentration must be based on the original sample volume, not the total mixed volume.

subtopic: Stereoisomerism: counting configurational isomers (stereocentres combined with geometric isomerism)
learningObjective: Enumerate the total number of stereoisomers of a molecule by identifying every independent stereogenic unit (stereocentres and stereogenic double bonds) and testing for internal symmetry.
stem: Consider the compound CH3–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–CH=CH–CH3 (hex-4-ene-2,3-diol). Taking into account every source of configurational isomerism in this molecule, what is the total number of distinct stereoisomers it can have?
explanation: The molecule has two stereocentres — C2 and C3, each bearing –OH, –H and two different chain fragments — and one stereogenic double bond, C4=C5, which is disubstituted with two different groups on each carbon and therefore shows E/Z isomerism. The two halves of the molecule are constitutionally different (a diol end versus a propenyl end), so there is no internal mirror plane and no meso reduction. The three independent stereogenic units multiply: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 distinct stereoisomers.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: two independent stereocentres (C2, C3) and one stereogenic double bond (C4=C5), with no molecular symmetry, give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 stereoisomers.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 4 = 2^2 counts only the two stereocentres and ignores that the disubstituted C=C is also stereogenic (E/Z) — the misconception that a carbon–carbon double bond never contributes to the stereoisomer count.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 6 assumes the two OH-bearing carbons are equivalent, giving 3 optical isomers (a meso form plus one enantiomeric pair) then ×2 for E/Z; the molecule has no internal symmetry, so no meso form exists.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 12 comes from 4 × 3, incorrectly treating the C=C as having three geometric states; a double bond has only two configurations (E and Z), contributing a single factor of 2.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 16 = 2^4 counts one stereogenic unit too many — for example treating each doubly-bonded carbon as a separate stereocentre; the whole C=C contributes just one factor of 2.

subtopic: Nucleophilic substitution: SN1 solvolysis rate and carbocation stability
learningObjective: Predict relative rates of nucleophilic substitution under ionising (SN1) conditions from the stability of the carbocation formed in the rate-determining step, distinguishing SN1 from SN2 steric logic.
stem: The following bromides are each dissolved in aqueous ethanol — a weakly nucleophilic, ionising solvent — at 25 °C, so that substitution proceeds essentially by an SN1 (solvolysis) mechanism. Which compound reacts fastest?
explanation: In SN1 the rate is set by the ionisation step, so it tracks the stability of the carbocation formed. Ionisation of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane gives a tertiary carbocation, the most stable in the set. A secondary (2-bromobutane) or primary (1-bromobutane) cation is less stable; the allyl cation is resonance-stabilised but only to roughly secondary-cation stability; and an aryl (sp2) C–Br bond does not ionise because a phenyl cation is prohibitively unstable. Hence the tertiary bromide solvolyses fastest.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: an aryl C–Br bond will not ionise under solvolytic conditions (a phenyl cation is enormously unstable); bromobenzene is essentially unreactive by SN1 despite the electron-rich ring.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: this applies SN2 steric reasoning (least-hindered substrate reacts fastest) to SN1 conditions; a primary carbocation is far too unstable to form readily, so 1-bromobutane is slow by SN1.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: ionisation yields a tertiary carbocation, the most stable of the options, giving the fastest rate-determining step and the fastest solvolysis.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: a secondary carbocation is more stable than primary but less stable than tertiary, so 2-bromobutane reacts more slowly than the tertiary bromide — a plausible but not the fastest choice.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: the allyl cation is resonance-stabilised but only to about secondary-cation stability, so it still ionises more slowly than the tertiary substrate — the misconception that any resonance stabilisation outperforms a tertiary centre.

subtopic: Amino acid acid–base behaviour: net charge and electrophoretic migration from pKa values
learningObjective: Determine the net charge of a polyprotic amino acid at a stated pH from its pKa values and predict its direction of migration in an electric field.
stem: Aspartic acid has pKa values of 2.0 (α-COOH), 3.9 (side-chain β-COOH) and 9.9 (α-NH3+). At pH 7.0, what is the predominant net charge on the molecule, and toward which electrode will it migrate during electrophoresis?
explanation: At pH 7.0 each group is compared with its pKa. Both carboxyls (pKa 2.0 and 3.9) lie well below the pH, so both are deprotonated (−1 each). The α-ammonium group (pKa 9.9) lies above the pH, so it remains protonated (+1). The net charge is (−1) + (−1) + (+1) = −1. A net-negative species is an anion and therefore migrates toward the positive electrode, the anode.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: −2 correctly deprotonates both carboxyls but forgets that the α-ammonium group (pKa 9.9) is still protonated (+1) at pH 7, which cancels one negative charge.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: +1 (cathode) overweights the ammonium group and treats only one carboxyl as ionised, or otherwise reverses the charge/electrode relationship.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: charges of −1, −1 and +1 sum to −1, and an anion migrates toward the anode (the positive electrode).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the net charge (−1) is right but the migration is reversed — anions travel to the anode, not the cathode; this is an electrode-sign confusion.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: a net charge of 0 assumes the molecule is at its isoelectric point at neutral pH; aspartate's pI ≈ (2.0 + 3.9)/2 ≈ 3.0, far below 7, so it is not neutral at pH 7.

subtopic: Carbohydrate chemistry: reducing sugars, the anomeric carbon and glycosidic linkage
learningObjective: Relate the reducing behaviour and mutarotation of a disaccharide to the presence or absence of a free anomeric (hemiacetal) carbon, independent of ring size or monosaccharide type.
stem: A disaccharide gives one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose on complete hydrolysis. Although both of these monosaccharides individually give a positive Tollens' test, the intact disaccharide gives a negative Tollens' test and shows no mutarotation in solution. Which structural feature best accounts for this behaviour?
choices: Its glycosidic bond joins the two anomeric carbons, so no free hemiacetal group remains
Both monosaccharide rings adopt the furanose form
It is built from two ketose units rather than two aldoses
It possesses no hydroxyl groups available for oxidation
explanation: Both reducing behaviour (Tollens'/Fehling's) and mutarotation require a free anomeric carbon that can ring-open to the acyclic carbonyl form. In this disaccharide (sucrose) the glucose C1 and the fructose C2 — both anomeric carbons — are locked together in the glycosidic bond, so neither ring can open and no aldehyde is exposed. Note that fructose is itself a reducing ketose; therefore the explanation must be the linkage, not the identity of the sugars.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: with both anomeric carbons committed to the glycosidic bond there is no hemiacetal left to ring-open, so no aldehyde forms — hence no reduction of Tollens' reagent and no mutarotation (exactly as in sucrose).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: β-linkages do not block reduction — lactose contains a β(1→4) bond yet is a reducing sugar because it retains a free anomeric carbon on its other ring.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: ring size (furanose versus pyranose) does not determine reducing ability; a free anomeric carbon in either ring form can still open and reduce.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: ketoses are not non-reducing; fructose gives a positive Tollens'/Fehling's test via base-catalysed isomerisation to an aldose, and the stem states fructose reduces Tollens'.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: the molecule has many free hydroxyl groups; reduction of the reagent is not generic –OH oxidation but oxidation of the specific hemiacetal/aldehyde at the anomeric carbon.

subtopic: E2 elimination: Zaitsev regiochemistry and enumeration of geometric-isomer products
learningObjective: Enumerate all constitutional and geometric alkene products of an E2 elimination and identify the major product using Zaitsev selectivity and relative alkene stability.
stem: 2-bromobutane is heated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, conditions favouring bimolecular (E2) elimination. Counting both constitutional and geometric (cis/trans) isomers, how many alkene products can form, and which one predominates?
explanation: β-Hydrogens are available on C1, whose removal gives terminal but-1-ene (no E/Z isomerism), and on C3, whose removal gives but-2-ene, which exists as both (E) and (Z). That is three distinct alkenes. Ethoxide is a small base, so E2 follows Zaitsev selectivity and the more-substituted but-2-ene dominates over but-1-ene; between its geometric isomers, (E)/trans is the more stable and is formed preferentially. Hence three products, with (E)-but-2-ene the major one.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: but-1-ene predominating reflects Hofmann (least-substituted) selectivity, which requires a bulky base; the small ethoxide base gives Zaitsev selectivity.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 'two products' overlooks that but-2-ene is formed as two separate geometric isomers (E and Z), and it also misassigns the major product.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: the three alkenes are but-1-ene, (E)-but-2-ene and (Z)-but-2-ene; Zaitsev favours the disubstituted but-2-ene and (E) is more stable than (Z), so (E)-but-2-ene predominates.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 'four products' incorrectly assigns E/Z isomers to terminal but-1-ene, whose terminal carbon bears two identical hydrogens and therefore shows no geometric isomerism.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: choosing (Z)-but-2-ene as major reverses geometric-isomer stability — the trans/(E) alkene is lower in energy and forms preferentially.

subtopic: Relative acidity of O–H and carboxylic acids: inductive and resonance effects
learningObjective: Rank organic Brønsted acids by comparing conjugate-base stabilisation from resonance and inductive effects, including the subtle ordering of activated phenols relative to carboxylic acids.
stem: Consider the five compounds: ethanol, phenol, 4-nitrophenol, ethanoic (acetic) acid and chloroethanoic (chloroacetic) acid. Which sequence correctly lists them in order of INCREASING acidity (weakest acid first)?
choices: ethanol < phenol < 4-nitrophenol < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid
phenol < ethanol < 4-nitrophenol < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid
ethanol < 4-nitrophenol < phenol < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid
ethanol < phenol < 4-nitrophenol < chloroethanoic acid < ethanoic acid
ethanol < phenol < ethanoic acid < 4-nitrophenol < chloroethanoic acid
explanation: Acidity tracks conjugate-base stability. Ethoxide (from ethanol) has no delocalisation and is weakest. Phenoxide is stabilised by ring resonance, so phenol is stronger. A para-nitro group withdraws electron density by resonance and induction, further stabilising the phenoxide, so 4-nitrophenol > phenol — yet it is still weaker than a carboxylic acid, whose carboxylate spreads the charge equally over two oxygens. Among the carboxylic acids, the electron-withdrawing chlorine in chloroethanoic acid stabilises the carboxylate inductively, making it stronger than ethanoic acid. Order of increasing acidity: ethanol < phenol < 4-nitrophenol < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: ethanol < phenol < 4-nitrophenol < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid follows increasing conjugate-base stabilisation — ring resonance, then –NO2 withdrawal, then symmetric carboxylate, then added –Cl induction.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: this ranks ethanol as a stronger acid than phenol; phenol is the stronger acid because its conjugate base is resonance-stabilised over the ring, whereas ethoxide is not.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: putting 4-nitrophenol below phenol implies the –NO2 group lowers acidity; an electron-withdrawing group stabilises the phenoxide and therefore increases acidity.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: making ethanoic acid stronger than chloroethanoic acid ignores (or reverses) chlorine's electron-withdrawing inductive effect, which stabilises the carboxylate and raises acidity.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this places 4-nitrophenol above ethanoic acid; a nitro-activated phenol (pKa ≈ 7) is still a weaker acid than a carboxylic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8), so it over-rates phenoxide resonance against carboxylate delocalisation.

subtopic: Strong acid–strong base neutralisation: pH from the excess reagent (dihydroxide base)
learningObjective: Determine the pH of a mixture of a strong monoprotic acid and a strong dihydroxide base by identifying the reagent in excess and dividing its remaining moles by the total volume.
stem: 200 mL of 0.30 M hydrochloric acid is mixed with 200 mL of 0.10 M barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂. Assuming volumes are additive and the temperature is 25 °C (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴), what is the pH of the resulting solution?
explanation: Count moles of each reactive ion. H⁺: 0.200 L × 0.30 M = 0.030 mol... note 0.200 × 0.30 = 0.060 mol H⁺. OH⁻: each Ba(OH)₂ furnishes two OH⁻, so 0.200 L × 0.10 M × 2 = 0.040 mol OH⁻. The strong acid and strong base neutralise 1:1, leaving excess H⁺ = 0.060 − 0.040 = 0.020 mol. The total volume is 200 + 200 = 400 mL = 0.400 L, so [H⁺] = 0.020 / 0.400 = 0.050 M and pH = −log(0.050) = 1.30. The key steps are (i) doubling the hydroxide for the dihydroxide base and (ii) dividing the leftover moles by the combined volume.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: excess H⁺ = 0.060 − 0.040 = 0.020 mol in 0.400 L gives [H⁺] = 0.050 M and pH = 1.30.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: assumes any strong-acid/strong-base mixture neutralises exactly to pH 7. Misconception: ignoring the stoichiometric excess and treating all neutralisations as complete and neutral.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: obtained by using the 0.020 mol of excess acid directly as the molarity (−log 0.020 = 1.70), i.e. never dividing by the 0.400 L total volume. Misconception: confusing moles of excess with concentration.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: obtained by counting only 0.020 mol OH⁻ (treating Ba(OH)₂ as though it gives one OH⁻ per formula unit), leaving 0.040 mol excess H⁺ and [H⁺] = 0.10 M. Misconception: failing to account for the two hydroxide ions released by each Ba(OH)₂.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: reverses the limiting reagent, treating the base as being in excess to give [OH⁻] = 0.050 M, pOH = 1.30 and pH = 12.70. Misconception: a sign/limiting-reagent error that assigns the excess to the wrong species.

subtopic: Solubility product: molar solubility of a 1:2 hydroxide under the common-ion effect
learningObjective: Compute the molar solubility of a sparingly soluble 1:2 hydroxide in a solution already containing the hydroxide ion, correctly applying the Ksp expression with its stoichiometric exponents.
stem: The solubility product of the hydroxide M(OH)₂ is Ksp = 4.0 × 10⁻¹² at 25 °C. What is the molar solubility of M(OH)₂ in a 0.20 M NaOH solution?
explanation: The dissolution is M(OH)₂ ⇌ M²⁺ + 2 OH⁻, so Ksp = [M²⁺][OH⁻]². In 0.20 M NaOH the hydroxide is overwhelmingly set by the added base, [OH⁻] ≈ 0.20 M (the small amount from the solid is negligible). The molar solubility equals [M²⁺], so s = Ksp / [OH⁻]² = 4.0 × 10⁻¹² / (0.20)² = 4.0 × 10⁻¹² / 0.040 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ M. The common ion suppresses solubility far below the value in pure water.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: obtained by dividing Ksp by [OH⁻] to the first power, 4.0 × 10⁻¹² / 0.20 = 2.0 × 10⁻¹¹. Misconception: omitting the square on [OH⁻], i.e. treating the salt as 1:1.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: obtained by taking s = √Ksp = √(4.0 × 10⁻¹²) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶, the form for a 1:1 salt, and ignoring the added NaOH entirely. Misconception: mis-writing the Ksp expression as a 1:1 salt and neglecting the common-ion effect.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: obtained by setting Ksp = s³ (i.e. Ksp = (s)(s)²) in water, giving s = (4.0 × 10⁻¹²)^{1/3} ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻⁴. Misconception: dropping the stoichiometric coefficient 2 when writing the Ksp expression (and ignoring the common ion).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this is the solubility in pure water, where Ksp = (s)(2s)² = 4s³ gives s = (Ksp/4)^{1/3} = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴. Misconception: ignoring the common-ion effect of the added NaOH.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: [OH⁻] ≈ 0.20 M from the NaOH, so s = Ksp/[OH⁻]² = 4.0 × 10⁻¹² / 0.040 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ M.

subtopic: Weak acid–strong base titration: equivalence-point pH and indicator selection
learningObjective: Predict that the equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration is basic, calculate its pH from conjugate-base hydrolysis, and select an indicator whose transition range brackets that pH.
stem: 25.0 mL of 0.10 M of a monoprotic weak acid HA (Ka = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶) is titrated with 0.10 M NaOH. Which statement correctly gives the pH at the equivalence point and an appropriate indicator? (Indicator ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4; methyl red 4.4–6.2; bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6; phenolphthalein 8.2–10.0; thymolphthalein 9.3–10.5.)
choices: pH ≈ 7.0, and bromothymol blue is a suitable indicator.
pH ≈ 10.7, and thymolphthalein is a suitable indicator.
pH ≈ 9.0, and methyl orange is a suitable indicator.
pH ≈ 5.2, and methyl red is a suitable indicator.
pH ≈ 9.0, and phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator.
explanation: At the equivalence point all HA has been converted to A⁻. Moles of A⁻ = 0.10 M × 0.0250 L = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol, now in 50.0 mL, so [A⁻] = 0.050 M. A⁻ is a weak base with Kb = Kw/Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹. Thus [OH⁻] = √(Kb·C) = √(2.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 0.050) = √(1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M, giving pOH = 5.00 and pH = 9.00. A good indicator changes colour across the steep region near pH 9, so phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) is appropriate.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: assumes the equivalence point is neutral (pH 7) and selects an indicator centred there. Misconception: treating every titration equivalence point as pH 7, forgetting that the conjugate base makes it basic.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: obtained by inserting Ka in place of Kb (no Kw conversion), giving [OH⁻] = √(Ka·C) ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁴ and pH ≈ 10.7. Misconception: using the acid dissociation constant directly as the base constant, overestimating the pH.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: the equivalence pH (≈9) is correct, but methyl orange changes colour at pH 3–4, far below the equivalence point, so it would signal the endpoint far too early. Misconception: matching the indicator to something other than the actual equivalence pH.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: obtained by treating the equivalence solution as if it still contained weak acid, [H⁺] = √(Ka·C) ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁴ (pH ≈ 3.3) or a related acidic estimate, and choosing an acid-range indicator. Misconception: applying the weak-acid formula to the fully neutralised (basic) solution.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: [A⁻] = 0.050 M, Kb = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹, [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M, pH = 9.00; phenolphthalein brackets this equivalence pH.

subtopic: Buffer capacity: maximum strong-acid load within a pH bound
learningObjective: Use the Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship to determine the maximum moles of strong acid a buffer can absorb before its pH crosses a specified bound, distinguishing the amount added from the resulting concentrations.
stem: A 1.0 L buffer is 0.80 M in sodium formate (HCOO⁻) and 0.20 M in formic acid (HCOOH), pKa = 3.75. Ignoring any volume change, what is the maximum amount of HCl (in mol) that can be added while keeping the pH at or above 3.75?
explanation: By Henderson–Hasselbalch, pH = pKa + log([HCOO⁻]/[HCOOH]). The condition pH ≥ pKa is equivalent to [HCOO⁻] ≥ [HCOOH]. Added H⁺ converts formate to formic acid mole-for-mole: after x mol HCl, [HCOO⁻] = 0.80 − x and [HCOOH] = 0.20 + x. The limiting case pH = pKa is when the two are equal: 0.80 − x = 0.20 + x, giving 0.60 = 2x, so x = 0.30 mol. Adding more than 0.30 mol makes formic acid the majority species and pushes the pH below 3.75. Hence the maximum is 0.30 mol.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 0.80 is the total amount of conjugate base present. Misconception: assuming the buffer keeps working until every mole of formate is consumed, ignoring that the pH falls below pKa well before that.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: setting 0.80 − x = 0.20 + x gives x = 0.30 mol, the largest HCl addition that keeps [HCOO⁻] ≥ [HCOOH] and thus pH ≥ pKa.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: obtained by using the pKa − 1 (10:1) limit, (0.80 − x)/(0.20 + x) = 1/10, which gives x ≈ 0.71 mol. Misconception: applying the general pKa ± 1 'useful buffer range' instead of the stated pH ≥ pKa condition.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.50 is the common concentration [HCOO⁻] = [HCOOH] = 0.50 M at the pH = pKa point, not the amount of acid added. Misconception: reporting the final species concentration instead of the moles of HCl introduced.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.60 is the initial excess of conjugate base over acid (0.80 − 0.20). Misconception: equating buffer capacity toward acid with the raw difference in initial amounts rather than solving for the 1:1 point.

subtopic: Selective (fractional) precipitation: residual ion fraction at the onset of the second precipitate
learningObjective: Determine the order of precipitation of two anions sharing a common cation and quantify the fraction of the first ion remaining when the second salt just begins to precipitate, using the correct Ksp exponents.
stem: A solution is 0.010 M in Cl⁻ and 0.010 M in CrO₄²⁻. Solid AgNO₃ is added slowly with stirring (no volume change). Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and Ksp(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹². What fraction of the original chloride remains in solution at the instant silver chromate just begins to precipitate?
explanation: AgCl starts to precipitate when [Ag⁺] = Ksp(AgCl)/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.010 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ M. Ag₂CrO₄ starts when [Ag⁺] = √(Ksp/[CrO₄²⁻]) = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹² / 0.010) = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ M. Because AgCl requires far less Ag⁺, it precipitates first. When [Ag⁺] rises to 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ M and chromate just begins to precipitate, the remaining chloride is [Cl⁻] = Ksp(AgCl)/[Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ M. The fraction remaining is 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ / 0.010 = 1.7 × 10⁻³ (about 0.17%), so the separation is nearly complete.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: obtained by dividing the onset [Ag⁺] (1.05 × 10⁻⁵) by the initial [Cl⁻] (0.010) to get ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³. Misconception: using the silver-ion concentration itself instead of computing the chloride that survives via Ksp(AgCl)/[Ag⁺].
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: at [Ag⁺] = 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ M (onset of Ag₂CrO₄), [Cl⁻] = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ M, so the fraction remaining is 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ / 0.010 = 1.7 × 10⁻³.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: obtained by comparing the two Ksp values directly (1.1 × 10⁻¹² < 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) and concluding Ag₂CrO₄ precipitates first, so chloride is untouched. Misconception: comparing Ksp magnitudes across salts of different stoichiometry without converting to the [Ag⁺] each requires.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: obtained by mishandling the 2:1 stoichiometry of Ag₂CrO₄ (an extra factor of 2 in [Ag⁺], e.g. [Ag⁺] ≈ 5.2 × 10⁻⁶), giving [Cl⁻] ≈ 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ M and a fraction ≈ 3.5 × 10⁻³. Misconception: an incorrect factor of 2 in the silver-chromate solubility expression.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this is the residual chloride concentration, 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ M, reported as though it were the fraction. Misconception: quoting the remaining molarity instead of dividing by the original 0.010 M to get a fraction.

subtopic: Solubility product with the common-ion effect
learningObjective: Apply the solubility product with a common ion to compute molar solubility and contrast it with solubility in pure water.
stem: The solubility product of silver chloride is Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. What is the molar solubility of silver chloride in a 0.10 mol L⁻¹ aqueous solution of sodium chloride?
explanation: For AgCl, Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]. The dissolved AgCl contributes s to each ion, but the chloride is dominated by the 0.10 mol L⁻¹ from NaCl (the common ion), so [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.10 and [Ag⁺] = s. Then s = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹. The molar solubility equals [Ag⁺] because each formula unit that dissolves releases one Ag⁺.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ divides Ksp by 0.01 instead of 0.10.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 4.2 × 10⁻⁶ has no basis in the Ksp expression for these values.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: s = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ is Ksp itself, not a solubility.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ is the solubility in PURE water (√Ksp), ignoring the common-ion suppression by the added chloride.

subtopic: Quantum numbers: counting the electrons in a ground-state atom that share a specified magnetic quantum number
learningObjective: Translate a ground-state electron configuration into the population of orbitals sharing a given magnetic quantum number, distinguishing orbitals from electrons.
stem: In a ground-state atom of zinc (Z = 30), how many of its electrons have a magnetic quantum number ml = 0?
explanation: Zinc has the ground-state configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶ 3s²3p⁶ 3d¹⁰4s², i.e. seven fully occupied subshells (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 3d, 4s). The magnetic quantum number ml labels individual orbitals within a subshell, and every subshell (whatever its value of l) contains exactly one orbital with ml = 0. Because all seven subshells are completely filled, each of these seven ml = 0 orbitals holds 2 electrons. Total = 7 × 2 = 14 electrons with ml = 0.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: excludes the filled 3d subshell, reflecting the misconception that d-subshells have only ml = ±1, ±2 and no ml = 0 orbital (6 subshells × 2 = 12).
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: over-counts the occupied subshells as eight (e.g. by wrongly assuming an occupied 4p subshell), giving 8 × 2 = 16.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: seven completely filled subshells, each contributing one ml = 0 orbital holding 2 electrons, gives 7 × 2 = 14.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: simply states the total number of electrons in the atom, ignoring the ml = 0 restriction entirely.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: counts the seven ml = 0 orbitals but records only one electron per orbital, forgetting that in the ground state of zinc every one of these orbitals is doubly occupied.

subtopic: Transition-metal ion electron configurations and number of unpaired electrons (paramagnetism)
learningObjective: Derive a first-row transition-metal ion configuration by removing 4s before 3d electrons and apply Hund's rule to count unpaired electrons.
stem: Which of the following gaseous ions, in its ground state, has exactly four unpaired electrons? (Assume the free ion adopts the arrangement of maximum multiplicity.)
explanation: For a first-row transition-metal ion the 4s electrons are removed before the 3d electrons. Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s², so Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶. Placing six electrons across the five 3d orbitals under Hund's rule gives one doubly occupied orbital and four singly occupied orbitals → four unpaired electrons. Checking the others: Cr³⁺ = 3d³ (3 unpaired), Mn²⁺ = 3d⁵ (5), Fe³⁺ = 3d⁵ (5), Ni²⁺ = 3d⁸ (2). Only Fe²⁺ gives four.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: Cr³⁺ is [Ar]3d³ with three unpaired electrons; chosen by a candidate who over-counts the d-electrons as 3d⁴.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: Fe²⁺ = [Ar]3d⁶; the six d-electrons occupy the orbitals as (↑↓)(↑)(↑)(↑)(↑), giving exactly four unpaired electrons.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Mn²⁺ is a half-filled 3d⁵ with five unpaired electrons; chosen by a candidate who pairs one electron and so fails to apply Hund's rule fully.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵ (five unpaired). This is the strongest trap: a candidate who removes only the two 4s electrons — forgetting the third electron is also lost, from 3d — obtains 3d⁶ and wrongly reads off four unpaired electrons.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Ni²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁸ with only two unpaired electrons; chosen by a candidate who ignores the forced pairing in a d⁸ set.

subtopic: Ionic radius across an isoelectronic series governed by effective nuclear charge
learningObjective: Rank an isoelectronic set of ions by radius using nuclear charge as the sole variable, and distinguish this from neutral-atom size trends.
stem: The ions P³⁻, S²⁻, Cl⁻, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ are all isoelectronic (each has 18 electrons). Which sequence lists them in order of increasing ionic radius?
explanation: All five species share the same 18-electron cloud, so the only variable is the nuclear charge pulling on it. As Z increases (P 15 → S 16 → Cl 17 → K 19 → Ca 20) the effective nuclear charge per electron rises and the radius contracts. Thus the smallest ion is the one with the most protons, Ca²⁺, and the largest is P³⁻: increasing radius is Ca²⁺ < K⁺ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < P³⁻.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: groups cations below anions (correct) but inverts the cations, treating fewer protons (K⁺) as giving a smaller ion — the reverse of the effective-nuclear-charge effect.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: orders the cations correctly but reverses the anions, reflecting the belief that a greater negative charge contracts rather than expands the ion.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: orders by increasing atomic number, reflecting the misconception that a larger nuclear charge produces a larger radius — the trend is exactly reversed.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: within an isoelectronic series radius decreases as nuclear charge increases, so Ca²⁺ (Z = 20) is smallest and P³⁻ (Z = 15) largest.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: uses neutral-atom radii (period-3 atoms smaller than period-4 K and Ca), ignoring that these are isoelectronic ions whose sizes are set by nuclear charge, not by periodic position.

subtopic: Bond-angle comparison: lone-pair count versus central-atom size and s–p mixing
learningObjective: Rank bond angles by combining lone-pair repulsion with the effect of central-atom size/electronegativity, recognising that lone-pair count alone is insufficient.
stem: Which of the following molecules has the smallest bond angle at its central atom?
explanation: BF₃ is trigonal planar (120°, no lone pairs) and CH₄ tetrahedral (109.5°). Adding lone pairs compresses the angle: NH₃ (one lone pair) ≈ 107° and H₂O (two lone pairs) ≈ 104.5°. H₂O and H₂S both have two lone pairs, so lone-pair count cannot separate them; the deciding factor is the central atom. Sulfur is larger and less electronegative than oxygen and uses almost pure p orbitals for bonding (little s–p mixing), giving an angle of about 92° — the smallest of the set.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: BF₃ is trigonal planar at 120°, the largest angle here; chosen by a candidate who assumes an electron-deficient, small central atom must force a small angle.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: H₂S has two lone pairs and a large, weakly electronegative sulfur atom bonding through nearly pure p orbitals, giving ≈92° — the smallest angle.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: CH₄ is 109.5°; chosen by a candidate who thinks four bonding pairs are the most crowded arrangement, overlooking that lone pairs push angles below the tetrahedral value.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: NH₃ is ≈107°; chosen by a candidate who correctly credits lone-pair compression but stops at one lone pair, missing the more compressed H₂O and H₂S.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: H₂O is ≈104.5°. This is the key trap — a candidate applying 'most lone pairs = smallest angle' picks H₂O and forgets that the larger central atom in H₂S drives its angle lower still.

subtopic: Hybridisation of atoms in a cumulated multiple-bond (cumulene/heterocumulene) system
learningObjective: Assign hybridisation to each heavy atom in a molecule by counting electron domains (sigma bonds plus lone pairs), correctly handling atoms bearing two cumulated double bonds.
stem: Methyl isocyanate has the connectivity H₃C–N=C=O. What are the hybridisation states of, respectively, the carbon of the CH₃ group, the nitrogen atom, and the central carbon atom (the one bonded to both N and O)?
explanation: Count electron domains (sigma bonds + lone pairs) on each atom. The CH₃ carbon forms four sigma bonds → four domains → sp³. The nitrogen is single-bonded to the CH₃ carbon and double-bonded to the central carbon, and carries one lone pair: two sigma bonds + one lone pair = three domains → sp² (bent at N). The central carbon has two cumulated double bonds (=N and =O): two sigma bonds and two pi bonds, giving only two domains → sp (linear N=C=O). Hence sp³, sp², sp.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: CH₃ carbon (4 sigma) is sp³; N (2 sigma + 1 lone pair) is sp²; the central carbon (2 sigma + 2 pi, two domains) is sp.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: treats N as sp³ (counting it as an ordinary amine and ignoring its pi bond) and the central carbon as sp²; reflects assigning hybridisation from lone pairs alone while overlooking multiple bonds.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: demotes the CH₃ carbon to sp², mis-counting its four sigma bonds — probably by association with the adjacent unsaturated system.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: treats N as sp, assuming it is linear like the central carbon and ignoring the lone pair that adds a third electron domain.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: correct for the first two atoms but labels the central carbon sp², failing to recognise that a carbon bearing two cumulated double bonds has only two electron domains and is sp.

subtopic: Intramolecular versus intermolecular hydrogen bonding and its effect on volatility (ortho/para isomers)
learningObjective: Explain a boiling-point difference between constitutional isomers by distinguishing intramolecular from intermolecular hydrogen bonding, rejecting molar-mass and polarity-cancellation explanations.
stem: 2-Nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol are structural isomers of formula C₆H₅NO₃ that differ only in the position of the –NO₂ group relative to the –OH group. 2-Nitrophenol is markedly more volatile (lower boiling point, readily steam-distilled) than 4-nitrophenol. Which statement best accounts for this difference?
choices: 4-Nitrophenol forms intramolecular hydrogen bonds that raise its boiling point above that of the ortho isomer.
In 2-nitrophenol the –OH and neighbouring –NO₂ form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, leaving fewer intermolecular hydrogen bonds, whereas 4-nitrophenol hydrogen-bonds intermolecularly.
2-Nitrophenol is non-polar because its –OH and –NO₂ bond dipoles cancel, so only weak dispersion forces act between its molecules.
4-Nitrophenol has the greater molar mass, so it experiences stronger London dispersion forces between molecules.
2-Nitrophenol ionises to a much greater extent in the liquid, and the resulting ion–ion attractions dominate its physical behaviour.
explanation: In the ortho isomer the –OH group sits next to the –NO₂ group, so the O–H can hydrogen-bond to an oxygen of the same molecule (a six-membered intramolecular chelate ring). This 'ties up' the O–H donor internally, sharply reducing molecule-to-molecule hydrogen bonding, so 2-nitrophenol is more volatile. In the para isomer the two groups are too far apart for an intramolecular bond, so every –OH hydrogen-bonds to neighbouring molecules, building an extended network that raises the boiling point.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: reverses the geometry (only the ortho isomer can hydrogen-bond intramolecularly) and the direction of the effect — intramolecular hydrogen bonding lowers, not raises, the boiling point.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: intramolecular hydrogen bonding in the ortho isomer removes hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors from the intermolecular pool, lowering its boiling point relative to the intermolecularly hydrogen-bonded para isomer.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: an ortho arrangement does not make the molecule non-polar — the bond dipoles do not cancel — and the volatility difference stems from hydrogen bonding, not from a loss of polarity.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: the two compounds are isomers with identical molecular formulae and therefore identical molar masses, so dispersion forces cannot be the distinguishing factor — a misconception that attributes any boiling-point gap to mass.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: conflates acidity/ionisation with volatility; the neutral molecular liquid, not an ionic lattice, governs the boiling point, and greater acidity would not lower it in this way.

subtopic: Standard free-energy change from cell potential (ΔG° = −nFE°) and spontaneity
learningObjective: Relate a standard cell potential to the standard Gibbs free-energy change using ΔG° = −nFE°, correctly identifying the number of electrons transferred in a balanced equation.
stem:
A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell operates by the overall reaction
2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l),   E°cell = +1.23 V at 298 K.
Taking the Faraday constant as F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹, what is the standard Gibbs free-energy change, ΔG°, for the reaction exactly as written?
explanation: First fix the number of electrons transferred in the reaction as written. Each H₂ is oxidised to 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻, so 2 H₂ release 4 electrons; O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ → 2 H₂O accepts them. Hence n = 4. Then ΔG° = −nFE° = −(4)(96 500 C mol⁻¹)(1.23 V) = −4.7478×10⁵ J ≈ −475 kJ. The value is large and negative, consistent with a spontaneous, energy-releasing fuel-cell reaction. The key skills are reading n from the balanced equation (not per mole of H₂ or per mole of water) and applying the negative sign so that a positive E° gives a negative ΔG°.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: used n = 2 (electrons per mole of H₂ or per mole of H₂O) instead of n = 4 for the reaction as written, halving the magnitude.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: overcounted the charge as n = 8 (e.g. one electron per hydrogen atom), doubling the true value.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: n = 4 electrons are transferred, so ΔG° = −(4)(96 500)(1.23) = −4.75×10⁵ J ≈ −475 kJ; negative, hence spontaneous.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: correct magnitude but positive sign — the negative sign in ΔG° = −nFE° was dropped, wrongly inferring a positive ΔG° from a positive E°.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: used n = 1, ignoring that four electrons are exchanged in the balanced equation.

subtopic: Equilibrium constant from standard cell EMF (ΔG° = −nFE° = −RT ln K)
learningObjective: Convert a standard cell potential into an equilibrium constant via log K = nE°/0.0592 at 298 K, avoiding sign, electron-count and ln-versus-log errors.
stem: For a certain galvanic cell the overall reaction transfers n = 2 electrons and has a standard cell potential E°cell = +0.30 V at 298 K. Given that (2.303 RT)/F = 0.0592 V at this temperature, the equilibrium constant K for the cell reaction is closest to:
explanation: Combine ΔG° = −nFE° with ΔG° = −RT ln K to get nFE° = RT ln K, i.e. log K = nE°/[(2.303RT)/F] = nE°/0.0592 at 298 K. Substituting: log K = (2)(0.30)/0.0592 = 0.60/0.0592 ≈ 10.1, so K ≈ 1×10¹⁰. A positive E° (spontaneous cell) must give K > 1, and the factor n = 2 roughly doubles the exponent compared with a one-electron cell.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: correct magnitude but negative exponent — a sign slip in ΔG° = −nFE°; a positive E° gives K ≫ 1, not K ≪ 1.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: used n = 1 (log K = 0.30/0.0592 ≈ 5), ignoring that two electrons are transferred.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: doubled the exponent (≈ 20), e.g. by applying the factor of 2 or the 2.303 term twice.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: used the natural-log constant RT/F ≈ 0.0257 V inside the base-10 expression, confusing ln K with log₁₀K.

subtopic: Second law: total entropy change of the universe and spontaneity (ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T)
learningObjective: Determine spontaneity from the total entropy change of the universe, correctly evaluating ΔS_surroundings = −ΔH/T and combining it with ΔS_system.
stem: A reaction carried out at a constant temperature of 300 K has ΔH = −120 kJ mol⁻¹ and a system entropy change ΔS_system = −200 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Using ΔS_surroundings = −ΔH/T, what is the total entropy change of the universe, and is the reaction spontaneous at 300 K?
explanation: The second law states a process is spontaneous when ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings > 0. The surroundings receive the released heat: ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T = −(−120 000 J mol⁻¹)/300 K = +400 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (watch the unit conversion kJ → J). Then ΔS_universe = −200 + 400 = +200 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ > 0, so the reaction is spontaneous at 300 K, even though the system's own entropy decreases. (It would become non-spontaneous only above 600 K, where |ΔS_surr| falls below 200.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: counted only ΔS_surroundings (+400) and neglected the negative system term.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: obtained the correct +200 but applied the second law backwards — a positive ΔS_universe means the reaction IS spontaneous.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: sign error — took ΔS_surr = +ΔH/T = −400 and added to −200.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: judged spontaneity from ΔS_system (−200) alone, ignoring the entropy exported to the surroundings.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T = +400, so ΔS_universe = −200 + 400 = +200 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ > 0; spontaneous.

subtopic: Predicting reaction direction from ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q by comparing Q with K
learningObjective: Predict the direction of a gas-phase reaction under non-standard conditions by evaluating the reaction quotient and comparing it with K (equivalently, the sign of ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q).
stem: The gas-phase reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g) has ΔG° = −11.4 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K, where (2.303 RT) = 5.71 kJ mol⁻¹. At a certain instant the partial pressures are p(HI) = 10 atm, p(H₂) = 0.10 atm and p(I₂) = 0.10 atm. In which direction does the reaction proceed, and why?
choices: No net reaction, because the two terms cancel (ΔG = 0)
To the right, because Q < K
To the left, because Q > K
explanation: Direction is set by ΔG = ΔG° + 2.303RT·log Q, not by ΔG° alone. From ΔG° = −2.303RT·log K: log K = 11.4/5.71 = 2.0, so K = 1×10². The quotient Q = p(HI)²/[p(H₂)·p(I₂)] = (10)²/(0.10 × 0.10) = 100/0.01 = 1×10⁴. Since Q (10⁴) > K (10²), ΔG = −11.4 + 5.71·log(10⁴) = −11.4 + 22.8 = +11.4 kJ mol⁻¹ > 0, so the forward reaction is non-spontaneous and the system shifts to the LEFT (net decomposition of HI) despite ΔG° being negative.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: faulty arithmetic — ΔG° = −11.4 and 2.303RT·log Q = +22.8 do not cancel; their sum is +11.4 kJ mol⁻¹.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: assumes Q equals K; here Q (10⁴) ≠ K (10²), so the system is not at equilibrium.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: judges direction from the standard free energy only; ΔG° fixes K, but the actual direction depends on ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q under the stated pressures.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: inverted the reaction quotient (reactants over products), giving Q < K and the opposite conclusion.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: Q = 10⁴ exceeds K = 10², making ΔG = +11.4 kJ mol⁻¹ > 0, so the reaction runs in reverse (to the left).

subtopic: Combining standard electrode potentials of half-reactions with different n via ΔG additivity
learningObjective: Derive an unknown standard electrode potential by adding the free energies (not the potentials) of two half-reactions that involve different numbers of electrons.
stem:
Given the standard electrode potentials E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V and E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V, calculate the standard electrode potential for the three-electron half-reaction
Fe³⁺(aq) + 3 e⁻ → Fe(s).
explanation: Electrode potentials are intensive, so they cannot simply be added or averaged when the electron numbers differ; the extensive quantity ΔG° = −nFE° is what adds. For Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺: ΔG₁° = −(1)F(0.77). For Fe²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Fe: ΔG₂° = −(2)F(−0.44). Summing gives Fe³⁺ + 3 e⁻ → Fe with ΔG₃° = ΔG₁° + ΔG₂° = −3FE₃°. Therefore E₃° = (n₁E₁ + n₂E₂)/(n₁ + n₂) = [(1)(0.77) + (2)(−0.44)]/3 = (0.77 − 0.88)/3 = −0.11/3 = −0.037 V.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: computed the correct ΔG-weighted numerator (1×0.77 + 2×(−0.44) = −0.11) but failed to divide by the total 3 electrons.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: added the two potentials directly, treating E° as an additive (extensive) quantity.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: since ΔG° adds, −3FE₃° = −1F(0.77) − 2F(−0.44), giving E₃° = (0.77 − 0.88)/3 = −0.037 V.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: weighted by electron number but swapped the weights (2 on +0.77 V and 1 on −0.44 V).
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: took the simple arithmetic mean (0.77 + (−0.44))/2, ignoring that the two steps involve different electron numbers.

subtopic: Faraday's laws: total gas volume from electrolysis of water with different electron stoichiometry at each electrode
learningObjective: Apply Faraday's laws to relate charge to moles of electrons and, using the differing electron counts of the cathode and anode half-reactions, compute the total volume of gases evolved during the electrolysis of water.
stem: A constant current of 5.00 A is passed through dilute sulfuric acid (electrolysis of water) for 32 min 10 s. The gases produced at both electrodes are collected at STP (molar volume 22.4 L mol⁻¹). Taking F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹, what is the TOTAL volume of gas (H₂ + O₂) evolved?
explanation: Charge passed: Q = I·t = 5.00 A × (32×60 + 10) s = 5.00 × 1930 = 9650 C, giving moles of electrons = 9650/96 500 = 0.100 mol. At the cathode, 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → H₂, so n(H₂) = 0.100/2 = 0.050 mol. At the anode, 2 H₂O → O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻, so n(O₂) = 0.100/4 = 0.025 mol. Total gas = 0.050 + 0.025 = 0.075 mol; at STP, V = 0.075 × 22.4 = 1.68 L. The crucial step is using the different electron counts (2 for H₂, 4 for O₂), which gives the characteristic 2:1 volume ratio of hydrogen to oxygen.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: counted only the cathode gas H₂ (0.050 mol → 1.12 L), omitting the oxygen at the anode.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: assumed equal moles of H₂ and O₂ (0.050 each → 0.100 mol), ignoring the different electron stoichiometry at the two electrodes.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: counted only the anode gas O₂ (0.025 mol → 0.56 L), omitting the hydrogen at the cathode.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: used incorrect electron counts (H₂ = 0.100 mol, O₂ = 0.050 mol → 0.150 mol), i.e. did not divide the charge correctly among the half-reactions.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: 0.100 mol e⁻ gives 0.050 mol H₂ (÷2) and 0.025 mol O₂ (÷4); total 0.075 mol × 22.4 = 1.68 L.

subtopic: Weakening an argument / confounding variable
learningObjective: Identify the statement that most undermines a causal conclusion drawn from a correlation.
stem: A large observational study found that adults who drink coffee regularly have a lower incidence of type 2 diabetes than adults who never drink coffee. On this basis, the authors concluded that drinking coffee protects against type 2 diabetes and recommended that all adults increase their coffee intake. Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument?
choices: A small proportion of adults are unable to tolerate the caffeine in coffee.
Regular coffee drinkers in the study were also considerably more likely to exercise frequently and to maintain a healthy body weight.
Coffee contains several antioxidant compounds whose biological effects are still being studied.
The risk of type 2 diabetes is also influenced by inherited genetic factors.
The participants in the study were recruited from a number of different countries.
explanation: The argument moves from a correlation (coffee drinkers have less diabetes) to a causal claim (coffee protects against diabetes). The claim is most weakened by evidence that a confounding variable could explain the correlation. If coffee drinkers also exercise more and stay leaner, their lower diabetes risk could be due to those healthy behaviours rather than the coffee itself, directly undermining the causal conclusion.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. Intolerance in a minority is about who can follow the advice, not about whether coffee is protective.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct. It introduces a confounding variable (exercise, healthy weight) that offers an alternative explanation for the correlation, weakening the causal claim.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. Suggesting a possible mechanism, if anything, mildly supports rather than weakens the claim.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. Additional genetic influences do not, by themselves, remove a genuine protective effect of coffee.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. A multi-country sample speaks to generalisability, not to whether coffee causes the effect.

subtopic: parallel reasoning
learningObjective: Identify the argument whose logical structure matches a given valid conditional-and-denial pattern, distinguishing it from superficially similar but structurally different arguments.
stem:
Every student who completes the summer laboratory placement is awarded a certificate of practical competence. Aylin did not complete the summer laboratory placement, so she will not be awarded a certificate of practical competence.

Which one of the following most closely parallels the reasoning used in the above argument?
choices: Only candidates who submit two references are considered for the post. Mara submitted two references, so she will be considered for the post.
Every applicant who scores above the threshold is invited to interview. Deniz scored above the threshold, so Deniz will be invited to interview.
Every member of the choir has passed the audition. Since Ela has not passed the audition, she is not a member of the choir.
Every resident of the north wing holds a parking permit. Kaan does not live in the north wing, so Kaan does not hold a parking permit.
Every book in the reference collection may be consulted only on the premises. This volume may be borrowed, so it is not part of the reference collection.
explanation: The original has the form: All A are B; x is not-A; therefore x is not-B. This is formally invalid (denying the antecedent), because being A is stated as sufficient for B but not as necessary — something could be B without being A. The parallel must reproduce exactly this structure: a universal 'all A are B', a premise that the subject is not-A, and a conclusion that the subject is not-B. Option D does this precisely: All north-wing residents hold a permit; Kaan is not a north-wing resident; therefore Kaan holds no permit — the identical denying-the-antecedent pattern (and the identical flaw). The correct parallel is judged by matching logical form, not by whether the reasoning is sound.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect: 'Only candidates who submit two references are considered' makes submitting references necessary, not sufficient, then affirms it to conclude eligibility — a different (and separately flawed) structure from the original.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect: this affirms the antecedent (All A are B; x is A; therefore x is B) — a valid form, the opposite structure to the flawed original.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect: this is denying the consequent / contrapositive (All A are B; x is not-B; therefore x is not-A) — a valid form, not the invalid denying-the-antecedent of the original.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: reproduces the exact form of the original — All A are B; the subject is not-A; therefore the subject is not-B (denying the antecedent) — including its flaw.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect: same valid contrapositive structure as B (reasons from the negation of the consequent back to the negation of the antecedent), so it does not match the invalid original.

subtopic: data interpretation with conditional proportions
learningObjective: Combine test-outcome proportions with false-positive and false-negative rates to recover the true prevalence of a condition in a screened population.
stem:
A clinic screens 900 people for a condition using a single test. Exactly 20% of those screened test positive. Of the people who test positive, one quarter do not actually have the condition (they are false positives). Of the people who test negative, one twenty-fourth actually do have the condition (they are false negatives).

How many of the 900 people screened actually have the condition?
explanation: Of 900 people, 20% test positive = 180, leaving 720 testing negative. Among the 180 positives, one quarter (45) are false positives, so the true positives — positives who really have the condition — number 180 − 45 = 135. Among the 720 negatives, one twenty-fourth (30) are false negatives who really do have the condition. The people who actually have the condition are the true positives plus the false negatives: 135 + 30 = 165. The key step is recognising that the truly affected are drawn from BOTH the positive group (minus false positives) and the negative group (the false negatives).

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect (135): counts only the true positives and forgets the false negatives hidden among those who tested negative.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect (210): adds all false results to the positives (180 + 30) or otherwise double-counts, treating every error as an additional case rather than reallocating them correctly.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect (150): a mixed slip — e.g. subtracting the false negatives (30) from the positives (180) instead of adding the false negatives to the true positives.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect (180): equates 'actually have the condition' with 'tested positive', ignoring both false positives and false negatives.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct (165): true positives (180 − 45 = 135) plus false negatives (720 ÷ 24 = 30) = 165.

subtopic: ordering / ranking deduction
learningObjective: Combine positional and relational constraints to deduce a unique finishing order and read off a specified position.
stem:
Five runners — Pia, Quinn, Rai, Sol and Tan — finished a race in positions first to fifth, with no ties. The following all hold:
- Exactly two runners finished ahead of Quinn.
- Pia finished neither first nor last.
- Quinn finished ahead of Sol.
- Rai and Sol did not finish in adjacent positions.
- Tan finished in the position immediately behind Rai.

Who finished fourth?
explanation: Exactly two ahead of Quinn fixes Quinn in 3rd. Quinn ahead of Sol means Sol is 4th or 5th. Rai and Sol are non-adjacent, and Tan is immediately behind Rai. Test Rai in 1st: then Tan is 2nd, leaving 4th and 5th for Pia and Sol; Pia cannot be last, so Pia is 4th and Sol is 5th. Check non-adjacency: Rai(1) and Sol(5) are not adjacent — valid. Any other placement of Rai fails: Rai in 2nd forces Tan into Quinn's 3rd slot; Rai in 4th forces Tan 5th, leaving Sol nowhere ahead-of-constraint-consistent and non-adjacent; Rai in 5th leaves no room for Tan behind. The unique order is Rai, Tan, Quinn, Pia, Sol, so fourth place is Pia.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect: 'exactly two ahead of Quinn' places Quinn third, not fourth — a common miscount treating the clue as 'two others' inclusively.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect: Rai must be first for the Tan and non-adjacency constraints to hold; placing Rai fourth breaks the Tan-immediately-behind clue.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect: Tan is immediately behind Rai in second place, not fourth; this confuses the Rai–Tan pairing's location.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect: Sol is fifth; solvers who read 'Quinn ahead of Sol' as 'Sol immediately after Quinn' wrongly place Sol fourth.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: the only consistent order is Rai(1), Tan(2), Quinn(3), Pia(4), Sol(5); Pia is fourth.

subtopic: underlying assumption / weaken integration
learningObjective: Identify the unstated assumption that a causal recommendation depends upon when it is inferred from an observed association between two variables.
stem:
A city recorded that neighbourhoods with more street trees have, on average, lower rates of hospital admission for respiratory illness than neighbourhoods with few street trees. A planning report concludes that the city should plant more street trees in the worst-affected neighbourhoods in order to reduce respiratory admissions there.

Which one of the following is an assumption on which the report's conclusion depends?
choices: Neighbourhoods with few street trees have the highest rates of respiratory admission in absolute terms.
Street trees are the single most important factor determining respiratory admission rates in any neighbourhood.
Planting street trees is less expensive than other measures the city might take to reduce respiratory illness.
The lower admission rates in leafier neighbourhoods are not explained mainly by some other factor that also happens to accompany the presence of street trees.
Residents of neighbourhoods with many street trees spend more time outdoors than residents of other neighbourhoods.
explanation: The report moves from an observed correlation (leafier neighbourhoods have fewer admissions) to a causal recommendation (planting trees will reduce admissions). For that leap to hold, the association must not be driven by a confounder — some third factor (e.g. wealth, lower traffic, better housing) that co-occurs with tree cover and is the real cause of the lower admissions. The argument therefore depends on assuming the relationship is not merely a by-product of such a confounding factor; the negation test confirms it: if the difference WERE explained by another accompanying factor, planting trees would not be expected to reduce admissions and the conclusion collapses. This is the classic correlation-versus-causation assumption.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect: this restates part of the data pattern and is not something the causal conclusion must presuppose; the recommendation could hold even if some leafy area had a high absolute rate.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect: the conclusion needs trees to have SOME causal effect, not to be the single most important factor — this overstates what the argument requires (too strong to be a necessary assumption).
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect: relative cost concerns policy choice, not whether planting trees will actually reduce admissions — irrelevant to the causal inference.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: ruling out a confounder that accompanies tree cover is exactly what the correlation-to-causation inference depends on; its negation destroys the argument.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect: this offers a possible mechanism but the argument does not require it, and if anything more outdoor time could increase exposure — it is not a needed assumption.

subtopic: short passage inference
learningObjective: Draw the single conclusion that must be true given a short passage, distinguishing entailed inferences from statements that are merely consistent with or plausibly suggested by the text.
stem:
Passage: In the regional library network, any title held in the rare-books room is never available for home loan. Every title that can be reserved online can be borrowed for home loan. Some titles in the folklore collection can be reserved online, and every title in the folklore collection is either in the rare-books room or in the open-access hall, but no title is in both.

Which one of the following must be true on the basis of the passage alone?
choices: Every title in the folklore collection can be reserved online.
At least one title in the folklore collection is held in the open-access hall.
Every title in the rare-books room belongs to the folklore collection.
No title in the folklore collection can be borrowed for home loan.
No title in the open-access hall can be reserved online.
explanation: Chain the conditionals. Rare-books titles are never home-loanable; online-reservable titles are all home-loanable; therefore no rare-books title can be reserved online (contrapositive).
