Some folklore titles CAN be reserved online, so those particular folklore titles are not in the rare-books room. Since every folklore title is in either the rare-books room or the open-access hall (and not both), any folklore title that is not in the rare-books room must be in the open-access hall. Hence at least one folklore title is in the open-access hall — option B is guaranteed. The other options either overgeneralise from 'some' to 'all', assert unsupported exclusivity, or reverse a conditional.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect: the passage says only that SOME folklore titles can be reserved online; inferring 'every' is an illicit some-to-all generalisation.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: the online-reservable folklore titles cannot be in the rare-books room (they are home-loanable), so by the exclusive either/or they must be in the open-access hall — at least one such title exists.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect: this reverses the relationship — the passage never says rare-books titles are drawn from the folklore collection.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect: the folklore titles that can be reserved online are precisely the ones that CAN be borrowed for home loan, so 'no folklore title can be borrowed' is false.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect: nothing forbids open-access-hall titles from being reservable online; the passage constrains rare-books titles, not open-access ones.

subtopic: Identifying the main conclusion
learningObjective: Distinguish the main conclusion of an argument from its premises and from the opposing view it rebuts.
stem: Some city planners argue that building more roads reduces traffic congestion. Experience in several large cities suggests the opposite. When a new motorway opens, journey times fall at first, but within a few years they return to their previous level. This happens because the additional capacity attracts drivers who previously used other routes, travelled at other times, or did not drive at all. The lower effective cost of driving therefore generates extra trips until congestion once again rises to the point where it deters further use. Building more roads is thus not an effective long-term cure for congestion. Which of the following best expresses the main conclusion of the argument?
choices: Additional road capacity attracts drivers who previously used other routes or travelled at other times.
The lower effective cost of driving generates extra car trips.
Building more roads is not an effective long-term cure for traffic congestion.
Some city planners believe that building more roads reduces congestion.
When a new motorway opens, journey times initially fall before rising again.
explanation: The main conclusion is the claim that all other statements are offered to support. Here it is flagged by the connective 'thus' and is the endpoint of the described feedback mechanism (induced demand). The other statements are the opposing view being rebutted, an intermediate observation, or links in the causal chain that explain why the conclusion holds.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: This states the mechanism by which the new capacity fills up and functions as a premise; it explains the conclusion rather than being it. Misconception: mistaking an explanatory premise for the main claim.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: This is a further link in the causal chain (induced demand) that supports the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. Misconception: selecting a causal sub-claim instead of the overall point.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: Signalled by 'thus', this is the claim that every other statement in the passage is marshalled to support.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: This is the opposing position that the author sets out to rebut, not the author's own conclusion. Misconception: taking the view introduced by 'some argue' as the argument's conclusion.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: This is an intermediate empirical observation describing only the short-term effect; it is evidence offered in support, not the point the argument establishes. Misconception: treating a supporting fact as the conclusion.

subtopic: Flaw: necessary versus sufficient condition
learningObjective: Identify reasoning that treats a necessary condition as though it were sufficient.
stem: The regulations state that, to be awarded a distinction in the diploma, a student must score at least 70% in the final examination. Marco scored 82% in the final examination. The examiner therefore concluded that Marco will certainly be awarded a distinction. Which of the following best identifies the flaw in the examiner's reasoning?
choices: It assumes that any student who scores below 70% must be denied a distinction.
It treats a condition that is only required for a distinction as though it were enough to guarantee one.
It generalises from Marco's performance to that of the other students in the cohort.
It relies on the examiner's authority rather than on the published marking regulations.
It draws a conclusion about a single individual from a rule that is meant to apply to a whole group.
explanation: The regulation gives a necessary condition: scoring at least 70% is required for a distinction. The examiner treats it as a sufficient condition — enough to guarantee the distinction — overlooking that other requirements could also apply. Confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one is the flaw.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: If 70% is genuinely necessary, then scoring below it does entail no distinction — a valid contrapositive, not a flaw. Misconception: mistaking a valid inference for an unwarranted assumption.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: Scoring at least 70% is stated only as a requirement (a necessary condition); the examiner wrongly treats it as sufficient to guarantee the distinction, ignoring possible further requirements.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: The conclusion is about Marco alone; no claim is made about other students. Misconception: mislabelling the error as a hasty generalisation.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: The examiner appeals to the marking regulation, not to personal authority. Misconception: mislabelling the error as an appeal to authority.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: A general rule can legitimately be applied to an individual, so this is not the error. Misconception: assuming that rules cannot be used to reason about single cases.

subtopic: Strengthening an argument (controlling confounders)
learningObjective: Recognise how matched groups and blinding strengthen a causal conclusion by removing confounders and bias.
stem: A pharmaceutical company claims that its new painkiller, Analgex, is more effective than the standard drug. In a clinical trial, patients who took Analgex reported greater pain relief on average than those who took the standard drug, and the company concluded that Analgex is the more effective painkiller. Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the company's conclusion?
choices: Analgex is considerably more expensive to manufacture than the standard drug.
A separate trial run by a different company found the standard drug to be highly effective.
Before the trial, patients in the Analgex group were told that they were receiving a promising new treatment.
The patients who took Analgex were, on average, several years younger than those who took the standard drug.
The two groups were closely matched for injury type and initial pain severity, and neither the patients nor the assessors knew which drug each patient received.
explanation: The conclusion is justified only if the greater average relief is due to the drug itself rather than to differences between the groups or to expectation effects. Matching the groups on relevant baseline factors and keeping both patients and assessors blind removes the main confounders and placebo/observer biases, so the observed difference is more credibly attributable to Analgex.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: Manufacturing cost is irrelevant to which drug relieves pain more effectively. Misconception: importing an irrelevant consideration into a claim about effectiveness.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: A separate finding that the standard drug works well says nothing about the head-to-head comparison in this trial. Misconception: treating an isolated fact about one drug as evidence for a comparative claim.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Telling patients they are receiving a promising treatment invites a placebo/expectation effect, providing an alternative cause and weakening the conclusion. Misconception: mistaking a bias-introducing factor for support.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: An age difference introduces a confounder that offers a rival explanation for the result, weakening rather than strengthening the conclusion. Misconception: assuming any extra detail about the treatment group supports the claim.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: Matched baseline characteristics plus double-blinding rule out confounding and placebo/observer effects, so the difference in reported relief is more plausibly caused by the drug.

subtopic: Matching / assignment deduction
learningObjective: Solve a constraint-based assignment puzzle by chaining deductions to a unique solution.
stem: Four colleagues — Ada, Ben, Cara and Dan — each ordered a different drink from the choices coffee, tea, juice and water. The following facts are known: Ada ordered neither coffee nor tea; Ben ordered neither juice nor water; Cara ordered tea; Dan did not order juice. Who ordered the water?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: Cara ordered tea. Ben ordered neither juice nor water, and tea is already taken, so Ben ordered coffee. That leaves juice and water for Ada and Dan. Dan did not order juice, so Dan ordered water and Ada ordered juice.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: The four constraints determine a unique solution, so the answer is fixed. Misconception: assuming the puzzle is under-determined without completing the chain of deductions.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: Ben is forced onto coffee, because he can take neither juice nor water and tea belongs to Cara. Misconception: overlooking that tea is already assigned when placing Ben.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: Cara is explicitly assigned tea. Misconception: misreading a fixed assignment given directly in the clues.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: Ben must take coffee, leaving juice and water for Ada and Dan; because Dan cannot take juice, Dan takes water.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Ada cannot take coffee or tea; once Ben takes coffee and Cara tea, Ada is left with juice or water, and since Dan cannot take juice, Ada must take juice, not water. Misconception: stopping before applying the constraint on Dan.

subtopic: Simpson's paradox / weighted-average reversal
learningObjective: Explain a rate reversal between aggregated and disaggregated data using differential case-mix (Simpson's paradox).
stem: A hospital reviews two surgeons. Overall, Surgeon X has a higher patient survival rate than Surgeon Y. However, when patients are split into 'high-risk' and 'low-risk' groups, Surgeon Y has a higher survival rate than Surgeon X within the high-risk group and also within the low-risk group. Which of the following, if true, best explains this apparent contradiction?
choices: Surgeon X treated a larger total number of patients than Surgeon Y.
Survival rates are generally higher for low-risk patients than for high-risk patients.
Within each risk group, Surgeon Y's survival rate exceeded Surgeon X's by only a small margin.
When the two surgeons' patients are combined, the high-risk group is larger than the low-risk group.
Surgeon Y operated on a much higher proportion of high-risk patients than Surgeon X did.
explanation: Surgeon Y can be better in every subgroup yet worse overall if Y's overall rate is a weighted average dominated by the low-survival high-risk patients. This occurs when Y treats a much larger share of high-risk patients than X does: the difference in case-mix, not surgical skill, drags Y's overall rate below X's. This is the mechanism of Simpson's paradox.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: The total number of patients does not by itself determine the direction of the averaged rates. Misconception: believing a larger sample alone can reverse a comparison.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: This is part of the setup (a background fact); on its own it does not explain why Y leads in both subgroups yet trails overall — that also requires a difference in case-mix between the surgeons. Misconception: mistaking a background premise for the explanation.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: The size of each within-group margin does not create the reversal; the reversal is produced by unequal weighting of the subgroups. Misconception: attributing the paradox to small subgroup differences rather than to case-mix.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: The combined-group composition is irrelevant; what matters is the difference in case-mix between the two surgeons, not the overall totals. Misconception: confusing the overall group size with the differential allocation between surgeons.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: If Y treats far more high-risk (low-survival) patients, Y's overall rate is a weighted average pulled down by that group, so Y can trail X overall while leading within each subgroup — the mechanism of Simpson's paradox.

subtopic: Distinguishing a warranted inference from an unsupported over-claim
learningObjective: Distinguish a conclusion that is logically forced by a short passage from unsupported over-claims, scope shifts, and counterfactuals.
stem:
A city council reviewed its cycling policy. Since a network of protected bike lanes was completed three years ago, the number of residents who commute by bicycle has risen by about 40%. In surveys, most of these new cyclists say they would not have started cycling without the protected lanes. The total number of cycling injuries reported in the city each year, however, is almost exactly the same as it was before the lanes were built.

On the basis of the passage alone, which of the following is most strongly supported?
choices: The average risk of injury per cyclist is now lower than it was before the lanes were built.
The protected lanes are the main reason the injury rate among cyclists has fallen.
Without the protected lanes, the number of cycling injuries in the city would have increased.
Most residents of the city now commute by bicycle.
Cycling in the city is now safer than driving.
explanation: The passage supplies two figures that can be combined: the number of cyclists rose by roughly 40%, while the total number of injuries stayed essentially constant. Spreading the same number of injuries over a substantially larger population of cyclists forces the per-cyclist injury rate down. That is the only option that follows from the stated facts. The other options each add something the passage does not license: a counterfactual, a mis-scaled quantifier, an unproven cause, or an absent comparison.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: with the total number of injuries unchanged but roughly 40% more cyclists, injuries per cyclist must be lower. This follows arithmetically from the two figures given, without adding any assumption.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: correlation-to-causation plus over-claim. The passage never isolates the lanes as the cause of any change and does not even state that the injury rate fell as a rate; other factors could contribute.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: unsupported counterfactual. The passage says nothing about what the injury count would have been without the lanes; it treats an untested 'what if' as established fact.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: scope/quantifier shift. 'Most of these new cyclists' is misread as 'most residents.' The passage only reports a ~40% rise in cycle commuting, not that a majority of the population now cycles.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: introduces an unstated comparison. Driving is never mentioned, so no claim about the relative safety of cycling versus driving can be supported by the passage.

subtopic: Normalising raw counts to a common rate before comparing
learningObjective: Compare two groups fairly by converting raw counts to a common rate and applying that rate to a different denominator.
stem: Clinic X carried out 1,200 operations last year and recorded 36 post-operative infections. Clinic Y carried out 400 operations in the same period and recorded 16 post-operative infections. The two clinics treat patients of comparable risk. If Clinic Y had achieved the same infection rate per operation as Clinic X, how many post-operative infections would Clinic Y have recorded?
explanation: First convert Clinic X's count to a rate: 36 / 1,200 = 0.03, i.e. a 3% infection rate per operation. Then apply that rate to Clinic Y's number of operations: 0.03 x 400 = 12 infections. The trap is that Clinic Y actually recorded a HIGHER rate (16 / 400 = 4%) than Clinic X despite fewer infections in absolute terms, so a fair comparison requires normalising to a common rate rather than comparing raw counts.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: Clinic X's rate is 36/1,200 = 3%; applying 3% to Clinic Y's 400 operations gives 0.03 x 400 = 12 infections.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: multiplies Clinic Y's 16 infections by 3 (the ratio of the clinics' sizes, 1,200/400) in the wrong direction, inflating the count instead of rescaling it to a common rate.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: reads Clinic X's infection rate of 3% as a raw count of '3 infections', confusing a percentage with a number.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: leaves Clinic Y's actual figure of 16 unchanged, failing to apply Clinic X's lower rate at all.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: gives the reduction (16 - 12 = 4), i.e. how many fewer infections would be needed, rather than the resulting number of infections that would be recorded.

subtopic: Truth-tellers and liars: self-referential statements and consistency testing
learningObjective: Solve a self-referential truth-teller/liar puzzle by testing each candidate assignment for internal consistency and eliminating those that contradict.
stem:
On a certain island, every inhabitant is either a truth-teller, who makes only true statements, or a liar, who makes only false statements. Three inhabitants make the following statements:

- Aldo says: 'Exactly one of the three of us is a truth-teller.'
- Bea says: 'Aldo is a liar.'
- Carlo says: 'Aldo and Bea are both liars.'

Which of the following must be true?
choices: Exactly one of them is a truth-teller, and it is Carlo.
None of them is a truth-teller.
Exactly one of them is a truth-teller, and it is Aldo.
Exactly two of them are truth-tellers.
Exactly one of them is a truth-teller, and it is Bea.
explanation: Test each possibility for consistency. Suppose Aldo is a truth-teller: then his statement is true, so there is exactly one truth-teller, namely Aldo, making Bea and Carlo liars. Check them: Bea (liar) says 'Aldo is a liar,' which is false as required; Carlo (liar) says 'Aldo and Bea are both liars,' which is false (Aldo is a truth-teller) as required. This assignment is fully consistent. Suppose instead Aldo is a liar: Bea's statement 'Aldo is a liar' is then true, so Bea is a truth-teller; Carlo's statement is then false, so Carlo is a liar; but that leaves exactly one truth-teller (Bea), which makes Aldo's statement TRUE — impossible for a liar. So the only self-consistent solution is Aldo = truth-teller, Bea = liar, Carlo = liar.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: making Carlo the truth-teller requires his statement 'Aldo and Bea are both liars' to be true, but in the valid solution Aldo is a truth-teller, so Carlo's statement is false and he cannot be the truth-teller.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: this assumes the statements form an unresolvable paradox. In fact a unique consistent assignment exists, so it is false that none of them is a truth-teller.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: checking all eight assignments, only Aldo = truth-teller, Bea = liar, Carlo = liar is self-consistent. Aldo's statement is true (he is the single truth-teller), and Bea's and Carlo's statements are both false, exactly as liars require.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: two truth-tellers would make Aldo's 'exactly one' statement false while he is supposedly truthful, a direct contradiction.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this corresponds to Aldo = liar, Bea = truth-teller, Carlo = liar, but that fails the consistency check: if Aldo is a liar, his statement 'exactly one is a truth-teller' becomes true (Bea alone), which a liar cannot truthfully assert.

subtopic: Flaw: survivorship / selection bias (sampling on the outcome)
learningObjective: Recognise survivorship (selection) bias: identify when a sample is defined by the very outcome under investigation, so failures are systematically excluded.
stem:
A financial columnist examined the managers of the ten largest investment funds in the country and found that all ten follow an aggressive, high-risk strategy. She concluded that an aggressive, high-risk strategy is the most reliable way to achieve strong long-term investment returns.

The columnist's reasoning is most vulnerable to the objection that:
choices: aggressive funds that performed badly would never have grown large enough to enter her sample, so failures are systematically excluded.
she treats the strategy used by the most successful funds as automatically the best one for others to copy.
she assumes the aggressive strategy caused the funds to grow large rather than merely accompanying their growth.
a sample of only ten funds is too small to support any general conclusion.
she does not specify what level of return should count as 'strong'.
explanation: The sample consists only of funds that have already become the largest — that is, only of survivors and successes. Any aggressive fund that pursued the same high-risk strategy and collapsed is, by construction, absent from the data. Because the evidence is filtered on the outcome (fund size, a marker of success), it cannot show that the strategy is reliable; it can only show that the strategy is common among those that happened to succeed. This is the defining structure of survivorship (selection) bias.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: this is survivorship (selection) bias. The sample is defined by an outcome — having become one of the largest funds — so aggressive funds that failed are invisible, and the surviving aggressive funds cannot establish that the strategy is reliable.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: this describes an appeal to success/popularity, but it merely restates the appeal of the conclusion rather than explaining why the evidence is unrepresentative of aggressive strategies in general.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: a correlation-versus-causation objection, tempting but off-target. Her conclusion is about long-term returns in general, and the decisive weakness is that her sample is drawn only from survivors, not that fund size was mis-attributed to the strategy.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: it blames the sample size, but the number ten is not the defect. Even the 100 largest funds would be filtered by the same success-based selection, so enlarging the sample would not remove the bias.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this attacks the vagueness of a term. Even if 'strong' were precisely defined, the underlying problem — that only surviving, successful funds were examined — would remain untouched.

subtopic: Base-rate reasoning and positive predictive value (conditional-probability inversion)
learningObjective: Combine prevalence, sensitivity and specificity to invert a conditional probability and compute the positive predictive value of a screening test.
stem: A screening test for a certain disease is used in a large population. The disease is present in 2% of the people screened. The test correctly returns a positive result in 90% of people who have the disease, and it wrongly returns a positive result in 5% of people who do not have the disease. A randomly screened person tests positive. Approximately what is the probability that this person actually has the disease?
explanation: Work with a concrete population of 10,000. Diseased: 2% = 200 people, of whom 90% test positive, giving 180 true positives. Healthy: 9,800 people, of whom 5% test positive, giving 490 false positives. Total positives = 180 + 490 = 670. The probability that a positive person truly has the disease is 180 / 670 ≈ 0.27, i.e. about 27%. Because the disease is rare, false positives from the large healthy majority swamp the true positives, so a positive result is more often wrong than right — a base-rate effect.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: gives the complementary probability, P(no disease | positive) = 490/670 ≈ 73% — the chance the person is disease-free — rather than the chance they have the disease.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: simply gives the prevalence (2%) and ignores the information supplied by the positive test result altogether.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: reports the test's sensitivity, P(positive | disease) = 90%, mistaking it for P(disease | positive) and ignoring the low base rate.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: among 10,000 people, 180 true positives arise from the 200 diseased (90%) and 490 false positives from the 9,800 healthy (5%); P(disease | positive) = 180/670 ≈ 27%.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: reports the specificity (95%), confusing the true-negative rate with the predictive value of a positive result.

subtopic: Principal flaw: equivocation (shift in the sense of a key term)
learningObjective: Identify equivocation as the principal flaw by testing whether a key term retains a single meaning across the premises and the conclusion.
stem:
A parent argues: 'Anyone who breaks the law deserves to be punished by the courts. My daughter broke her solemn promise to practise the piano every evening, and a promise one makes to oneself is a kind of personal law. Therefore my daughter deserves to be punished by the courts.'

Which of the following identifies the principal flaw in this argument?
choices: It treats a condition that is merely necessary for court punishment as though it were sufficient for it.
It relies on the word 'law' in two different senses, so the premises do not connect as the argument requires.
It takes for granted, in one of its premises, the very claim that the argument sets out to establish.
It assumes that because something has not been shown to be permitted, it must therefore be forbidden.
It presents only two possibilities when others are available, forcing a false choice between them.
explanation: The argument turns on the word 'law'. In the first premise 'law' means the law of the state, breach of which can bring court punishment. The bridging premise then redefines 'law' as a self-imposed personal rule (a promise to oneself). Because the key term carries two different meanings, the premises fail to link up: nothing about breaking a personal resolution entails liability to the courts. The test for equivocation is whether a crucial term keeps a single, consistent meaning throughout; here it does not. Distractor D is tempting, but the breakdown is not about a necessary/sufficient confusion — it is the meaning shift itself that severs the inference.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: although breaking a law may be necessary but not sufficient for court punishment, the decisive error is the shift in the meaning of 'law', not a confusion of a conditional relationship. Misconception: diagnosing a necessary/sufficient error whenever a conclusion feels too strong.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: this is equivocation. 'Law' denotes a state statute in the first premise and a self-imposed rule in the bridging premise; the inference is valid only if one meaning is held constant, which it is not.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: this describes circular reasoning, but the conclusion is not smuggled into the premises. Misconception: treating every invalid argument as though it must beg the question.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this is the argument from ignorance, but nothing here reasons from a lack of evidence. Misconception: matching the argument to a familiar fallacy label that does not fit its actual structure.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this describes a false dilemma, but the argument never restricts matters to two options. Misconception: assuming that any argument reaching a harsh conclusion must be forcing a false choice.

subtopic: Identifying a necessary (unstated) assumption via the negation test
learningObjective: Isolate the unstated assumption on which an argument depends by applying the negation test to a causal claim drawn from a comparison case.
stem:
A city councillor argues: 'Installing average-speed cameras along our ring road will reduce the number of serious-injury collisions on it. We know this because, on the comparable ring road of a neighbouring city, the number of serious-injury collisions fell by 40% in the two years after such cameras were introduced.'

The councillor's argument depends on assuming which of the following?
choices: Average-speed cameras lower the speed of every vehicle on the ring road to below the legal limit.
No city that has ever installed average-speed cameras has subsequently seen its collision figures rise.
Serious-injury collisions on the neighbouring city's ring road have continued to fall in every year since the cameras were introduced.
The 40% fall on the neighbouring ring road was brought about by the cameras rather than by other road-safety changes made there at the same time.
The financial cost of installing the cameras is outweighed by the value of the collisions they prevent.
explanation: The conclusion — cameras will cut serious-injury collisions on this ring road — rests entirely on the evidence that collisions fell after cameras were installed elsewhere. For that evidence to support the conclusion, the earlier fall must actually have been caused by the cameras rather than by some other change introduced at the same time. Apply the negation test: suppose the 40% fall had really been caused by other safety measures; then the neighbouring case would give no reason to expect cameras to help here, and the argument would collapse. Because negating E destroys the argument, E is a necessary assumption. The other options are either irrelevant to the conclusion (B), or far stronger than the argument requires (A, C, D).

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: the conclusion needs only that collisions fall, not that every vehicle is slowed below the limit; this overstates the required mechanism. Misconception: mistaking a strong sufficient-sounding mechanism for the assumption the argument actually needs.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: a universal claim about every city that has ever installed cameras is far stronger than a single comparison needs. Misconception: confusing a necessary assumption with an unnecessary sweeping generalisation.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: only the initial two-year fall is used as evidence, so a continued year-on-year decline is not required. Misconception: over-reading the evidence as though it depended on a sustained trend.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: this is the bridging assumption. If the fall had been caused by other simultaneous changes, the evidence would not transfer to this city; its negation defeats the argument, so it must be assumed.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: cost-effectiveness is beside the point, since the conclusion claims only a reduction in collisions, not that the scheme is worth the money. Misconception: importing a practical consideration the conclusion never makes.

subtopic: Principal flaw: fallacy of composition (part-to-whole inference)
learningObjective: Recognise the fallacy of composition, distinguishing an invalid part-to-whole inference from other named reasoning errors.
stem:
A financial adviser argues: 'I have examined these ten technology companies one by one, and each is individually a sound investment with strong fundamentals. It follows that a fund holding an equal stake in all ten of them must be a sound and well-diversified investment.'

Which of the following best describes the principal flaw in this reasoning?
choices: It assumes that a characteristic possessed by each individual member of a collection must also be a characteristic of the collection taken as a whole.
It draws a sweeping conclusion about technology companies in general from a sample far too small to be representative.
It uses the word 'sound' with one meaning in its premises and a subtly different meaning in its conclusion.
It concludes that one event must have caused another purely from the observation that the two are correlated.
It presents investing in these ten companies as the only available course of action, ignoring other options.
explanation: The adviser moves from 'each part (company) is sound' to 'the whole (the fund) is sound and well-diversified'. That is the fallacy of composition: a property of the individual members need not carry over to the collection they form. In fact ten individually sound technology firms are likely to be highly correlated, so the fund could look sound yet be badly undiversified and risky — which is exactly why part-to-whole transfer is not valid in general. The flaw is structural and holds independently of any finance knowledge.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: this is the fallacy of composition — it infers a feature of the whole collection from a feature shared by each of its members, an inference that is not generally valid.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: the argument does not generalise from a sample to all technology companies; it reasons about these specific ten. Misconception: mistaking a part-to-whole inference for a sample-to-population one.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 'sound' carries the same meaning throughout, so there is no equivocation. Misconception: seeing a shift in the meaning of a term where the term is in fact used consistently.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: no causal claim is drawn from a correlation here. Misconception: defaulting to the most familiar fallacy (correlation implies causation) regardless of the argument's actual form.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: the argument does not falsely narrow the options to a single choice. Misconception: mislabelling a structural inference error as a false dilemma.

subtopic: Absolute vs relative risk reduction and the number needed to treat
learningObjective: Distinguish relative risk reduction from absolute risk reduction and compute the number needed to treat from trial incidence data.
stem: In a five-year randomised trial, the risk of suffering a first heart attack was 4% among patients given a placebo and 3% among patients given drug Z. A newspaper reports: 'Drug Z cuts the risk of a heart attack by 25%.' Assuming the trial results are valid, which single statement is best supported by these figures?
choices: Treating one hundred patients with drug Z for five years prevents, on average, one heart attack.
Drug Z prevents a heart attack in 25% of the patients who take it.
Among patients taking drug Z, the chance of a heart attack is 25 percentage points lower than among those taking the placebo.
Without drug Z, one in four patients would suffer a heart attack within five years.
Treating four patients with drug Z for five years prevents, on average, one heart attack.
explanation: 'Cuts risk by 25%' is a relative risk reduction: (4% − 3%)/4% = 25%. What determines how many people actually benefit is the absolute risk reduction, 4% − 3% = 1 percentage point = 0.01. The number needed to treat is 1/ARR = 1/0.01 = 100, so roughly one heart attack is prevented for every 100 patients treated for five years. The wrong options each mistake the relative figure for an absolute one or a baseline: A reads 25% as the share of patients who benefit, B reads it as a 25-point absolute drop, E reads it as the baseline incidence, and C uses the relative figure inside the NNT formula (1/0.25 = 4).

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: the number needed to treat is 1/ARR = 1/0.01 = 100, so on average one heart attack is prevented per hundred patients treated for five years.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: this interprets the 25% relative reduction as the proportion of treated patients in whom a heart attack is prevented; in fact only about 1% (one in a hundred) benefit. Misconception: reading a relative risk reduction as an absolute proportion of patients helped.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: this conflates a 25% relative reduction with a 25 percentage-point absolute reduction; the absolute gap is only 1 point (4% versus 3%). Misconception: confusing 'percent' with 'percentage points'.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: this treats the 25% relative figure as the baseline five-year incidence, whereas the placebo baseline is 4%. Misconception: mistaking a relative reduction for the underlying risk.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: this computes the number needed to treat from the relative reduction, 1/0.25 = 4, instead of from the absolute reduction. Misconception: dividing 1 by the relative rather than the absolute risk reduction.

subtopic: Deductive selection puzzle with conditional/biconditional constraints (necessity across all valid models)
learningObjective: Solve a deductive selection puzzle with conditional and biconditional constraints and determine which conclusion holds across every valid arrangement.
stem:
Exactly which of five friends — Nia, Omar, Pia, Raj and Tom — will go on a weekend trip is governed by the following facts:
- If Nia goes, then Omar goes.
- Pia goes if and only if Nia does not go.
- Exactly one of Omar and Raj goes.
- If Pia goes, then Raj goes.
- Tom goes if and only if both Omar and Pia go.

Which one of the following must be true?
choices: Tom does not go on the trip.
Raj does not go on the trip.
If Omar goes on the trip, then Pia goes on the trip.
Exactly three of the five friends go on the trip.
explanation: The third fact forces exactly one of Omar and Raj, giving two cases. Case 1 (Omar in, Raj out): 'If Pia goes then Raj goes' forces Pia out; 'Pia if and only if not Nia' then forces Nia in; 'If Nia then Omar' is satisfied; 'Tom if and only if both Omar and Pia' gives Tom out because Pia is out. Arrangement: Nia and Omar go, the rest stay. Case 2 (Omar out, Raj in): 'If Nia then Omar' forces Nia out; 'Pia if and only if not Nia' forces Pia in; 'If Pia then Raj' is satisfied; 'Tom if and only if both Omar and Pia' gives Tom out because Omar is out. Arrangement: Pia and Raj go, the rest stay. Both valid arrangements exclude Tom and contain exactly two members, so the only statement true in every arrangement is that Tom does not go.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: in both valid arrangements at least one of Omar and Pia is absent, so 'both Omar and Pia go' is never satisfied and Tom is excluded in every case.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: Raj goes in Case 2 (Omar out, Raj in), so his exclusion is not forced. Misconception: fixing on the single arrangement in which Raj happens to be out.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: in Case 1, Omar goes but Pia does not, making the conditional false, so it is not a necessary truth. Misconception: mis-deriving 'if Omar then Pia' from the rules that actually link Pia to Nia and Raj.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: each valid arrangement contains exactly two members, not three. Misconception: a miscount, or assuming more constraints must mean more people selected.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: Nia goes in Case 1 but stays home in Case 2, so her going is not forced. Misconception: treating something that can be true in one arrangement as though it must be true in all.

subtopic: Absolute-value equations
learningObjective: Solve an absolute-value equation by splitting into cases and count the distinct real solutions.
stem: How many distinct real values of x satisfy the equation |x² − 4| = 3 ?
explanation: The equation splits into two cases. Case 1: x² − 4 = 3 ⇒ x² = 7 ⇒ x = ±√7 (two real solutions). Case 2: x² − 4 = −3 ⇒ x² = 1 ⇒ x = ±1 (two more real solutions). Because √7 ≈ 2.65 and 1 are all distinct, there are four distinct real solutions in total.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct. ±√7 and ±1 give four distinct real roots.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 3 would require one repeated root, but none of the four values coincide.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. Solutions clearly exist, so 0 is wrong.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 2 results from solving only the case x² − 4 = 3 (or only x² = 1).
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. 1 ignores that each x² value yields two opposite roots.

subtopic: Combinatorial probability with 'at least'
learningObjective: Compute an 'at least' probability using combinations and the complement rule.
stem: A committee of 4 people is chosen at random from a group of 5 men and 4 women. What is the probability that the committee contains at least 2 women?
explanation: The total number of committees is C(9,4) = 126. Use the complement of 'fewer than 2 women': committees with 0 women = C(5,4) = 5; committees with exactly 1 woman = C(4,1)·C(5,3) = 4·10 = 40. So committees with at least 2 women = 126 − 5 − 40 = 81. The probability is 81/126 = 9/14.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. 3/7 = 54/126 does not match any correct combination of the cases.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 20/63 = 40/126 is the probability of exactly one woman only.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 5/14 = 45/126 is the probability of the complement (0 or 1 woman) after simplification error.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. 2/3 = 84/126 slightly over-counts and is not obtained from the correct case analysis.

subtopic: Change-of-base substitution in a logarithmic equation
learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by reducing it to a quadratic through a substitution and combine the roots.
stem: Consider the equation log₂(x) + logₓ(2) = 5/2, defined for x > 0 with x ≠ 1. What is the product of all real solutions of this equation?
explanation: Let t = log₂(x). By change of base logₓ(2) = 1/log₂(x) = 1/t, so the equation becomes t + 1/t = 5/2, i.e. 2t² − 5t + 2 = 0, giving t = 2 or t = 1/2. Hence x = 2² = 4 or x = 2^(1/2) = √2, both valid (positive, ≠ 1). Their product is 4·√2 = 4√2. Equivalently, the product equals 2^(t₁+t₂) = 2^(5/2) = 4√2.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: x = 4 and x = √2 give a product of 4√2 = 2^(5/2).
optionAnalysis.B: Keeps only t = 2 and squares it, or multiplies the exponents (2 · 1/2 mishandled) to reach 2³ = 8.
optionAnalysis.C: Keeps only the root t = 1/2, reporting the single solution √2.
optionAnalysis.D: Uses the product of the t-values (2 · 1/2 = 1) as an exponent: 2¹ = 2, misapplying the exponent law.
optionAnalysis.E: Adds the two solutions (4 + √2) instead of multiplying them.

subtopic: Hypergeometric probability without replacement
learningObjective: Compute a probability for sampling without replacement using combinations rather than independent trials.
stem: A box contains 12 electronic components, of which exactly 4 are defective. Three components are drawn at random simultaneously (that is, without replacement). What is the probability that exactly one of the three drawn components is defective?
explanation: Because the draws are simultaneous, use combinations. Favourable outcomes = choosing 1 of the 4 defective and 2 of the 8 good: C(4,1)·C(8,2) = 4·28 = 112. Total outcomes = C(12,3) = 220. Probability = 112/220 = 28/55. Independent-trial (with-replacement) reasoning is invalid here because the composition changes with each draw.

optionAnalysis.A: Uses C(4,1)/C(12,3) = 4/220 = 1/55-type slip, omitting the C(8,2) factor (here rounded to 4/55).
optionAnalysis.B: Halves the favourable count (uses C(8,2)/2 or forgets the factor 2 in a pair count), giving 56/220 = 14/55.
optionAnalysis.D: Treats draws as independent with p = 1/3 defective: 3·(1/3)(2/3)² = 27/64-style with-replacement error.
optionAnalysis.E: Simply reports the defective fraction 4/12 = 1/3, ignoring the 'exactly one of three' condition.

subtopic: Counting real solutions of an absolute-value quadratic equation
learningObjective: Solve an equation containing an absolute value of a quadratic by case analysis and discard extraneous roots.
stem: How many distinct real solutions does the equation |x² − 4| = x + 2 have?
explanation: First, the right side must be non-negative, so x ≥ −2. Case 1 (|x| ≥ 2, where x² − 4 ≥ 0): x² − 4 = x + 2 ⇒ x² − x − 6 = 0 ⇒ x = 3 or x = −2; both satisfy x ≥ −2 and x² − 4 ≥ 0, so both are valid. Case 2 (|x| < 2, where x² − 4 < 0): −(x² − 4) = x + 2 ⇒ x² + x − 2 = 0 ⇒ x = 1 or x = −2; only x = 1 lies in |x| < 2 (x = −2 is a boundary already counted). The distinct valid solutions are x = −2, 1, 3 — three in total.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: valid roots are x = −2, 1, 3, giving three distinct solutions.
optionAnalysis.B: Counts all four algebraic roots (3, −2, 1, −2) without noticing x = −2 repeats and without the x ≥ −2 check.
optionAnalysis.C: Discards x = −2 for wrongly requiring x > −2 (strict), keeping only x = 3 or only x = 1.
optionAnalysis.D: Concludes no solution by assuming |x² − 4| can never equal a linear expression, skipping case analysis.
optionAnalysis.E: Solves only the case x² − 4 = x + 2 (roots 3 and −2), missing the sign-flipped case that yields x = 1.

subtopic: Law of cosines with the circumradius (law of sines)
learningObjective: Integrate the law of cosines and the law of sines to find the circumscribed-circle radius of a triangle.
stem: In triangle ABC the angle at vertex A measures 60°, the side AB = 8 and the side AC = 5. What is the radius of the circle circumscribed about the triangle?
explanation: The side opposite A is BC = a. By the law of cosines, a² = AB² + AC² − 2·AB·AC·cos 60° = 64 + 25 − 2·8·5·(1/2) = 89 − 40 = 49, so a = 7. By the law of sines, 2R = a/sin A = 7/sin 60° = 7/(√3/2) = 14/√3, hence R = 7/√3 = 7√3/3.

optionAnalysis.A: Uses R = a·(√3/2)/... i.e. multiplies by sin A instead of dividing, giving 7√3/2.
optionAnalysis.B: Uses 2R = a/sin A but reports 2R = 14/√3 = 14√3/3 as R, forgetting to halve.
optionAnalysis.C: Divides by an extra factor of 2, using R = a/(4 sin A) and getting 7√3/6.
optionAnalysis.D: Sets R = a/2 = 7/2, forgetting the sin A denominator (treating a as a diameter).
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: a = 7 and R = a/(2 sin A) = 7/√3 = 7√3/3.

subtopic: Exponential equation reducible to a quadratic
learningObjective: Solve an exponential equation by substitution and sum its real solutions.
stem: What is the sum of all real solutions x of the equation 2^(2x) − 5·2^x + 4 = 0 ?
explanation: Let u = 2^x (so u > 0). The equation becomes u² − 5u + 4 = 0, which factors as (u − 1)(u − 4) = 0, giving u = 1 or u = 4. Then 2^x = 1 ⇒ x = 0, and 2^x = 4 ⇒ x = 2. Both are valid (u > 0). The sum of the solutions is 0 + 2 = 2.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 5 is the sum of the roots in u (1 + 4), not the sum of the x-values.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 3 does not correspond to the solution set.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 6 mis-solves 2^x = 4 as x = 4 or similar.
optionAnalysis.D: CORRECT: the solutions are x = 0 and x = 2, summing to 2.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0 is only one of the two solutions (x = 0), not their sum.

subtopic: Probability of an even product (complement)
learningObjective: Compute the probability of an even product using the complement (all-odd) and combinations.
stem: Two distinct integers are chosen at random from the set {1, 2, 3, …, 10}. What is the probability that their product is even?
explanation: The product is even unless BOTH chosen numbers are odd. There are 5 odd numbers {1,3,5,7,9}, so the number of all-odd pairs is C(5,2) = 10, out of C(10,2) = 45 total pairs. P(product odd) = 10/45 = 2/9, so P(product even) = 1 − 2/9 = 7/9.

optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 5/9 does not follow from the correct count of pairs.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 2/9 is the probability the product is ODD (both numbers odd), i.e. the complement.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 4/9 mis-counts the favourable or total pairs.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 1/2 assumes even/odd are equally likely, ignoring that only an all-odd pair gives an odd product.

subtopic: Sum of an infinite geometric series (repeated-dose steady state)
learningObjective: Model a repeated-dose accumulation process as an infinite geometric series and evaluate its steady-state sum.
stem: A patient is treated with a drug taken as a single 60 mg dose at the same time every day. Over each 24-hour interval the body eliminates 75% of the drug present, so that just before the next dose only 25% of the previous amount remains in the body. Assuming this pattern continues indefinitely, what amount of drug is present in the body immediately after a dose is taken in the long-term (steady) state?
explanation: Let L be the amount present immediately after a dose in the steady state. Each day the previous amount decays to 25% of itself, then a fresh 60 mg is added, so at equilibrium L = 60 + 0.25 L. Hence 0.75 L = 60 and L = 80 mg. Equivalently, the doses form an infinite geometric series 60 + 60(0.25) + 60(0.25)^2 + ... with first term 60 and ratio r = 0.25, summing to 60/(1 − 0.25) = 80 mg.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: takes the steady-state level to equal a single dose (60 mg), ignoring the drug carried over from previous doses — i.e. omitting the accumulation entirely.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: reports the trough level just before the next dose (0.25 × 80 = 20 mg), misreading 'immediately after' as 'immediately before'.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: at equilibrium L = 60 + 0.25L gives L = 60/(1 − 0.25) = 80 mg, the sum of the infinite geometric series with a = 60, r = 0.25.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses the eliminated fraction r = 0.75 instead of the retained fraction 0.25 in the sum, giving 60/(1 − 0.75) = 240 mg.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: adds only the first two doses (60 + 0.25×60 = 75 mg), truncating the geometric series after two terms instead of summing it to its limit.

subtopic: Vieta's formulas: sum of squares of the roots of a cubic
learningObjective: Apply Vieta's formulas to evaluate a symmetric function (the sum of the squares) of the roots of a cubic without solving it.
stem: Let p, q and r be the three roots (real or complex) of the cubic equation 2x^3 − 3x^2 + 4x − 5 = 0. What is the value of p^2 + q^2 + r^2?
explanation: For 2x^3 − 3x^2 + 4x − 5 = 0, Vieta's formulas give p + q + r = 3/2, pq + pr + qr = 4/2 = 2, and pqr = 5/2. Using the identity p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = (p + q + r)^2 − 2(pq + pr + qr) = (3/2)^2 − 2(2) = 9/4 − 4 = −7/4. (The value is negative because two of the roots are complex conjugates; the symmetric function is nonetheless real.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: computes only (p + q + r)^2 = (3/2)^2 = 9/4, forgetting to subtract the 2(pq + pr + qr) term.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: divides only the sum of roots by the leading coefficient but forgets to divide the pairwise sum, giving (3/2)^2 − 2(4) = −23/4.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = (3/2)^2 − 2(2) = 9/4 − 4 = −7/4, applying Vieta's formulas with the leading coefficient 2.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: reads the coefficients directly as the symmetric sums (sum = 3, pairwise sum = 4), ignoring the leading coefficient 2, giving 3^2 − 2×4 = 1.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: uses the wrong sign, (p + q + r)^2 + 2(pq + pr + qr) = 9/4 + 4 = 25/4, adding rather than subtracting the pairwise term.

subtopic: Rational inequality solved by sign analysis
learningObjective: Solve a rational inequality by collecting terms on one side and analysing the sign of the resulting quotient, respecting domain restrictions.
stem: Determine the complete solution set of the inequality (2x − 1)/(x + 3) ≥ 1.
explanation: Move everything to one side: (2x − 1)/(x + 3) − 1 ≥ 0, i.e. (2x − 1 − (x + 3))/(x + 3) ≥ 0, which simplifies to (x − 4)/(x + 3) ≥ 0. The critical values are x = 4 (numerator zero, included) and x = −3 (denominator zero, excluded). A sign chart shows the quotient is positive for x < −3 and for x > 4, and equals 0 at x = 4. Hence the solution set is (−∞, −3) ∪ [4, +∞).

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: multiplies both sides by (x + 3) as if it were always positive, obtaining 2x − 1 ≥ x + 3 → x ≥ 4, and loses the branch where the denominator is negative.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: includes x = −3, but there the denominator is zero and the expression is undefined, so −3 must be excluded.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: rearranging gives (x − 4)/(x + 3) ≥ 0; the quotient is non-negative for x < −3 or x ≥ 4, so the solution is (−∞, −3) ∪ [4, +∞).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: excludes x = 4, but the inequality is non-strict (≥) and the numerator (x − 4) is zero there, so x = 4 must be included.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: selects the interval between the critical values, where the quotient is actually negative — the sign of the quotient has been reversed.

subtopic: System of exponential equations via common-base exponents
learningObjective: Solve a system of exponential equations by rewriting each term to a common base and equating exponents to form and solve a linear system.
stem: Real numbers x and y satisfy the system: 2^x · 8^y = 2^11 and 9^x / 3^y = 3. What is the value of x + y?
explanation: Rewrite with common bases. First equation: 2^x · 2^(3y) = 2^(x + 3y) = 2^11, so x + 3y = 11. Second equation: 3^(2x) / 3^y = 3^(2x − y) = 3^1, so 2x − y = 1. From the second, y = 2x − 1; substituting: x + 3(2x − 1) = 11 → 7x − 3 = 11 → x = 2, and then y = 3. Therefore x + y = 5.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: treats 8^y as 2^y (dropping the exponent 3 in 8 = 2^3), so the first equation reads x + y = 11 directly.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: rewriting to bases 2 and 3 gives x + 3y = 11 and 2x − y = 1, whose solution is x = 2, y = 3, so x + y = 5.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: solves the system correctly to x = 2, y = 3 but reports x alone instead of the requested sum x + y.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: simply adds the two right-hand exponents (11 from 2^11 and 1 from 3^1) to get 12, without solving the system.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: treats 9^x as 3^x (dropping the exponent 2 in 9 = 3^2), giving the second equation as x − y = 1 and hence x + y = 6.

subtopic: Interplay of arithmetic and geometric progressions
learningObjective: Combine the defining conditions of arithmetic and geometric progressions to determine an unknown common ratio.
stem: In an arithmetic progression with non-zero common difference, the first term is 3, and the first, second and fifth terms are (in that order) three consecutive terms of a geometric progression. What is the common ratio of that geometric progression?
explanation: Let the arithmetic progression have first term a = 3 and common difference d. The first, second and fifth terms are a, a + d and a + 4d. For these to be consecutive terms of a geometric progression, (a + d)^2 = a(a + 4d). Expanding: a^2 + 2ad + d^2 = a^2 + 4ad, so d^2 − 2ad = 0, i.e. d(d − 2a) = 0. Since d ≠ 0, d = 2a = 6. The three geometric terms are 3, 9, 27, so the common ratio is 27/9 = 9/3 = 3.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: computes d/a = 6/3 = 2, confusing the relationship between the common difference and the first term with the geometric common ratio.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: the geometric condition gives d = 6, producing terms 3, 9, 27 with common ratio 9/3 = 3.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: inverts the ratio, dividing an earlier term by a later one (3/9) instead of a later term by an earlier one.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: reports the second geometric term (a + d = 9) itself rather than the ratio between successive terms.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: reports the common difference d = 6 of the arithmetic progression instead of the common ratio of the geometric progression.

subtopic: Infinite geometric series: sum and sum of squares
learningObjective: Set up and solve simultaneous equations from the sum and the sum of squares of an infinite geometric series.
stem: An infinite geometric series has first term a and common ratio r with |r| < 1. The sum of the series is 9, and the sum of the squares of its terms is 40.5. What is the value of the common ratio r?
explanation: The sum of the series is a/(1 − r) = 9. The squares of the terms form a geometric series with first term a² and ratio r², so their sum is a²/(1 − r²) = 40.5. Substituting a = 9(1 − r) into the second equation: [9(1 − r)]²/(1 − r²) = 81(1 − r)²/[(1 − r)(1 + r)] = 81(1 − r)/(1 + r) = 40.5. Hence (1 − r)/(1 + r) = 0.5, giving 1 − r = 0.5 + 0.5r, so 1.5r = 0.5 and r = 1/3. (Check: a = 6, sum = 6/(2/3) = 9; sum of squares = 36/(8/9) = 40.5.)

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/9 confuses r with r² or misreads the ratio of the two sums.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: r = 1/4 comes from mishandling the 1 − r² factorisation (e.g. treating it as (1 − r)²).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: r = 2/3 makes the terms fall off too slowly; the sum of squares would exceed 40.5.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: r = 1/2 gives (1 − r)/(1 + r) = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3, not 0.5, so the sum of squares would not be 40.5.

subtopic: Power of a point: tangent–secant relationship from an external point
learningObjective: Apply the power-of-a-point (tangent–secant) theorem to relate a tangent length to a secant line and extract the interior chord.
stem: From a point P outside a circular pond, a straight walkway PT of length 8 m runs to the point T where it just touches (is tangent to) the edge of the pond. A second straight walkway from P crosses the pond, meeting the edge first at A and then at B, with PA = 4 m. What is the length AB, the distance across the pond along this walkway?
explanation: For a tangent PT and a secant through A and B drawn from the same external point P, the power of the point gives PT² = PA·PB. Thus 8² = 4·PB, so PB = 64/4 = 16 m. AB is the chord between the two intersection points: AB = PB − PA = 16 − 4 = 12 m.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: gives PB, the full distance from P to the far edge (or applies PT² = PA·AB), forgetting that AB is measured from A, so the external segment PA must be subtracted.
optionAnalysis.B: Correct: PT² = PA·PB gives PB = 16 m, hence the chord AB = PB − PA = 12 m.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: adds PA + PB = 4 + 16, treating the answer as the total secant path from P through B.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: takes the arithmetic mean of PA and PB, (4 + 16)/2 = 10, with no geometric justification.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: reports the tangent length PT (8 m) itself as the chord, ignoring the power-of-a-point relation entirely.

subtopic: Length of a chord cut on a circle by a line via the perpendicular distance from the centre
learningObjective: Determine the length of a chord cut on a circle by a line using the perpendicular distance from the centre and the Pythagorean relationship.
stem: A circle has equation x² + y² − 2x − 4y − 20 = 0. Find the length of the chord that the line 3x + 4y = 26 cuts on this circle.
explanation: Completing the square gives (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² = 25, so the centre is (1, 2) and the radius r = 5. The perpendicular distance from the centre to the line 3x + 4y − 26 = 0 is |3(1) + 4(2) − 26|/√(3² + 4²) = |−15|/5 = 3. The half-chord is √(r² − d²) = √(25 − 9) = 4, so the full chord length is 2 × 4 = 8.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: returns the half-chord √(r² − d²) = 4, forgetting to double it to obtain the full chord.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: assumes the line passes through the centre and returns the diameter, 2r = 10.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: computes 2√(r² + d²), adding d² instead of subtracting it in the Pythagorean step.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses 2d = 6, mistaking twice the centre-to-line distance for the chord length.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: chord = 2√(r² − d²) = 2√(25 − 9) = 8.

subtopic: Trigonometric equation via the double-angle identity
learningObjective: Solve a trigonometric equation by reducing a double-angle term to a quadratic in cosine and count all solutions on a given interval.
stem: Determine the number of values of x in the interval [0, 2π) that satisfy cos 2x + cos x = 0.
explanation: Using cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1, the equation becomes 2cos²x + cos x − 1 = 0, which factors as (2cos x − 1)(cos x + 1) = 0. So cos x = 1/2 or cos x = −1. On [0, 2π), cos x = 1/2 gives x = π/3 and x = 5π/3, while cos x = −1 gives x = π. That is three solutions in total.

optionAnalysis.A: Correct: the roots are x = π/3, x = π, and x = 5π/3 — three solutions.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: mis-expands cos 2x (mixing 1 − 2sin²x with cos terms) and picks up an extra spurious root.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: keeps only one factor (e.g. cos x = 1/2), overlooking the cos x = −1 branch.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: counts cos x = −1 as producing two solutions in the interval, whereas it yields only x = π.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: counts every root of the quadratic in cos over a doubled range such as 0 ≤ x < 4π.

subtopic: Combining the area formula with the cosine rule; selecting the obtuse-angle case
learningObjective: Integrate the triangle area formula with the cosine rule, selecting the correct obtuse-angle solution to determine a side.
stem: In triangle ABC, AB = 8, AC = 5, and the area of the triangle is 10. Given that angle A is obtuse, find BC².
explanation: Area = ½·AB·AC·sin A = ½·8·5·sin A = 20 sin A = 10, so sin A = 1/2. Since A is obtuse, A = 150° and cos A = −√3/2. By the cosine rule, BC² = AB² + AC² − 2·AB·AC·cos A = 64 + 25 − 2·8·5·(−√3/2) = 89 + 40√3.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: uses the acute solution A = 30° (cos A = +√3/2), giving 89 − 40√3, and so ignores the stated condition that A is obtuse.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: sets cos A = −1/2, confusing the value of sin A with cos A; this gives 89 + 2·40·(1/2) = 129.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: with cos A = −√3/2, BC² = 89 + 40√3.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: omits the −2·AB·AC·cos A term (equivalently treats A as 90°), leaving just 64 + 25 = 89.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: drops the factor of 2, using AB·AC·cos A instead of 2·AB·AC·cos A, giving 89 + 20√3.

subtopic: Radius of a sphere inscribed in a right circular cone via the inradius of the axial cross-section
learningObjective: Find the radius of a sphere inscribed in a cone by identifying it with the inradius of the axial cross-sectional triangle.
stem: A right circular cone has base radius 5 cm and vertical height 12 cm. A sphere is inscribed in the cone so that it touches the base and the entire lateral surface. What is the radius of the sphere?
explanation: The slant height is √(5² + 12²) = 13 cm. Cutting the cone through its axis gives an isosceles triangle with base 2R = 10, two equal sides of 13, and height 12. The inscribed sphere's radius equals the inradius of this triangle: r = Area / semiperimeter = (½·10·12) / ((10 + 13 + 13)/2) = 60/18 = 10/3 cm.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: takes half the base radius, R/2 = 5/2, wrongly assuming the sphere spans half the base width.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: divides the cross-section area by the full perimeter instead of the semiperimeter, 60/36 = 5/3.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: uses Rh/(R + h) = 60/17, substituting the vertical height for the slant length in the tangency relation.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: uses Rh/L = 60/13, an incorrect similar-triangle ratio.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct: the sphere's radius is the inradius of the axial section, 60/18 = 10/3 cm.

subtopic: Circles tangent to both coordinate axes through a fixed point; two-solution locus
learningObjective: Model a circle tangent to both coordinate axes with centre (r, r), solve the resulting quadratic, and compute the distance between the two solution centres.
stem: In the coordinate plane, a circle lies in the first quadrant, is tangent to both the x-axis and the y-axis, and passes through the point (2, 1). Two such circles exist. What is the distance between their centres?
explanation: A circle in the first quadrant tangent to both axes has centre (r, r) and radius r. Passing through (2, 1): (2 − r)² + (1 − r)² = r². Expanding gives r² − 6r + 5 = 0, so r = 1 or r = 5. The centres are (1, 1) and (5, 5), and the distance between them is √((5 − 1)² + (5 − 1)²) = √32 = 4√2.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: mis-solves the quadratic as r = 1, 3, placing centres at (1, 1) and (3, 3) and giving 2√2.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: places the centres at (0, 0) and (6, 6) (radii mis-added into the coordinates), giving 6√2.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: distance = √(4² + 4²) = 4√2.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: takes only one coordinate difference, 5 − 1 = 4, ignoring the second dimension of the distance.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: adds the two radii, 1 + 5 = 6, instead of finding the distance between the centres.

subtopic: Expected value of a discrete random variable: fair price of a prize-draw ticket
learningObjective: Compute the expected value of a discrete random variable and use it to determine the mathematically fair price of a lottery or prize-draw ticket.
stem: A charity organises a prize draw with 200 numbered tickets, each equally likely to be drawn. The prizes are: one prize worth €300, four prizes worth €50 each, and ten prizes worth €10 each; every remaining ticket wins nothing, and no single ticket can win more than one prize. The organisers wish to set the ticket price equal to the expected winnings of a single ticket (a mathematically 'fair' price). What price should they charge per ticket?
explanation: The expected winnings of one ticket is the sum of each prize value multiplied by the probability that this ticket wins it. Each ticket has probability 1/200 of being the one drawn for any particular prize, so E = 300·(1/200) + 50·(4/200) + 10·(10/200) = 1.50 + 1.00 + 0.50 = €3.00. Equivalently, the total prize money (300 + 4·50 + 10·10 = €600) shared over the 200 tickets gives 600/200 = €3.00. The fair price is €3.00.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: divides the €600 total prize money by the number of prizes (15) instead of the number of tickets (200), confusing the average prize won by a winner with the expected value of an arbitrary ticket.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: counts only the €300 grand prize (300/200 = 1.50) and ignores the €50 and €10 prizes — the expected value must sum the contribution of every prize, not just the largest.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: includes the grand prize and the four €50 prizes ((300 + 200)/200 = 2.50) but forgets the ten €10 prizes; all prize tiers contribute to the expected value.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: E = 300·(1/200) + 50·(4/200) + 10·(10/200) = 1.50 + 1.00 + 0.50 = €3.00, equal to the €600 total prize money divided by 200 tickets.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: divides the €600 total prize money by 100 rather than by the 200 tickets — a misreading of the number of tickets in the draw.

subtopic: Permutations of a multiset with a non-adjacency restriction (gap method with identical letters)
learningObjective: Count arrangements of a multiset subject to a non-adjacency restriction using the gap (slot) method, applying a combination rather than a permutation for identical objects.
stem: The seven letters A, A, A, B, C, D, E are arranged in a row to form strings (the three A's are identical to one another, so two strings are the same if they read identically). In how many of these arrangements are no two A's adjacent to one another?
explanation: First arrange the four distinct non-A letters B, C, D, E in a row: 4! = 24 ways. These four letters create five gaps (one before, three between, one after) into which A's may be placed. To keep the A's apart, place at most one A in each gap, so choose 3 of the 5 gaps; because the A's are identical this is a combination, C(5,3) = 10. Total = 24 × 10 = 240.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 5! = 120 treats the three A's as a single block 'AAA', giving five items to arrange — this counts arrangements where the A's are all together, the exact opposite of the requirement.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 840 = 7!/3! is the total number of distinguishable arrangements with no restriction at all, ignoring the non-adjacency condition.
optionAnalysis.C: Correct: 4! ways to arrange B, C, D, E (=24) times C(5,3) ways to place the three identical A's in the five gaps (=10) gives 24 × 10 = 240.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 1440 = 24 × P(5,3) treats the three identical A's as distinguishable, using the permutation P(5,3) = 60 instead of the combination C(5,3) = 10.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 600 is the complementary count (arrangements in which at least two A's are adjacent), obtained as 840 − 240; the question asks for the non-adjacent arrangements themselves.

subtopic: Bayes' theorem: posterior probability of the source given a defective item
learningObjective: Apply the law of total probability and Bayes' theorem to compute the posterior probability of a source given observed evidence.
stem: A workshop assembles a component using two machines. Machine X assembles 60% of the components and 2% of its output is defective; Machine Y assembles the remaining 40% and 5% of its output is defective. A finished component is selected at random from the combined output and found to be defective. What is the probability that it was assembled by Machine Y?
explanation: By the law of total probability, P(defective) = 0.60·0.02 + 0.40·0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. By Bayes' theorem, P(Y | defective) = P(Y and defective)/P(defective) = 0.020/0.032 = 0.625.

optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 0.400 is the prior P(Y); it ignores the defective evidence entirely instead of updating on it.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 0.050 is P(defective | Y), the defect rate of Machine Y; this inverts the conditional, confusing P(Y | defective) with P(defective | Y).
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.375 = 0.012/0.032 is P(X | defective), the posterior for the other machine; the question asks for Machine Y.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.020 is the joint probability P(Y and defective); it omits the final step of dividing by P(defective) to normalise.

subtopic: Binomial distribution: cumulative 'at least k' probability under random guessing
learningObjective: Model repeated independent trials with the binomial distribution and compute a cumulative 'at least k' probability by summing the relevant terms.
stem: A multiple-choice quiz has 5 questions, each with 4 answer options exactly one of which is correct. A student who has not studied answers every question by guessing independently at random. The quiz is passed only by answering at least 4 of the 5 questions correctly. What is the probability that this student passes?

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/256 = (1/4)^4 drops the binomial coefficient C(5,4) and the fifth question's factor, treating 'four correct' as a single fixed outcome.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 1/1024 = (1/4)^5 counts only the all-five-correct outcome and omits the exactly-four-correct case, which also passes.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 15/1024 counts only P(X=4) and omits P(X=5); passing requires 'at least 4', so both cases must be added.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 3/16 comes from using p = 1/2 (as if each question had two options): P(X≥4) with p=1/2 = (5+1)/32 = 6/32 = 3/16; here each question has four options, so p = 1/4.

subtopic: Derangements: probability of exactly one fixed point in a random permutation
learningObjective: Combine a combination with a derangement count to find the probability of exactly one fixed point in a uniformly random permutation.
stem: In a class, five students each hand in a homework sheet labelled with their own name. The teacher shuffles the five sheets thoroughly and returns them at random, one to each student, with every ordering equally likely. What is the probability that exactly one student receives their own sheet?
explanation: There are 5! = 120 equally likely orderings. For exactly one fixed point, first choose which student gets their own sheet: C(5,1) = 5 ways. The remaining four sheets must all go to the wrong students, i.e. be a derangement of 4 objects, and the number of such derangements is D₄ = 9. So the count is 5 × 9 = 45, giving probability 45/120 = 3/8.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/5 treats 'exactly one of five' as a plain 1-in-5 chance, ignoring the requirement that the remaining four sheets must all be misplaced.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong: 1/3 = 40/120 uses an incorrect derangement count D₄ = 8 instead of the correct 9, so (5 × 8)/120 = 1/3.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 3/40 = 9/120 = D₄/5! omits the factor C(5,1) for choosing which of the five students is the one fixed point.
optionAnalysis.D: Correct: choose the single fixed student (C(5,1) = 5) and derange the other four (D₄ = 9): (5 × 9)/120 = 45/120 = 3/8.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 11/30 = 44/120 = D₅/5! is the probability that NO student receives their own sheet (a full derangement), which is a different event.

subtopic: Hypergeometric probability: exactly k successes without replacement
learningObjective: Compute the probability of exactly k successes in draws without replacement using combinations.
stem: A bag contains 4 red marbles and 6 blue marbles, identical apart from colour. Three marbles are drawn at random, all at once (without replacement). What is the probability that exactly two of the three drawn marbles are red?
explanation: Choosing 3 marbles from 10 can be done in C(10,3) = 120 equally likely ways. 'Exactly two red' means choosing 2 of the 4 red marbles and 1 of the 6 blue marbles: C(4,2) × C(6,1) = 6 × 6 = 36. The probability is 36/120 = 3/10.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 1/5 = 24/120 miscounts the favourable outcomes (e.g. C(4,2)×C(6,1) done incorrectly).
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 1/6 treats the draws as if order mattered or uses the wrong denominator.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 2/5 = 48/120 over-counts the favourable selections.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 3/5 is far too large and corresponds to no correct combination count.

subtopic: Change of momentum on rebound
learningObjective: Apply the impulse–momentum theorem to a rebounding object, handling the change of direction correctly.
stem: A 0.20 kg ball travelling horizontally at 10 m/s strikes a rigid vertical wall head-on and rebounds horizontally at 8.0 m/s in the opposite direction. The ball is in contact with the wall for 0.020 s. What is the magnitude of the average force exerted by the wall on the ball?
explanation: Take the initial direction as positive. The ball's momentum changes from +(0.20)(10) = +2.0 kg·m/s to −(0.20)(8.0) = −1.6 kg·m/s because it reverses direction. The change in momentum is Δp = −1.6 − (+2.0) = −3.6 kg·m/s, magnitude 3.6 kg·m/s. The average force is |Δp|/Δt = 3.6 / 0.020 = 180 N.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. 20 N comes from using the difference in speeds (10 − 8 = 2 m/s) and ignoring the direction reversal.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 100 N corresponds to bringing the ball only to rest from 10 m/s (Δp = 2.0), not to rebounding.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. 360 N doubles the correct impulse, e.g. by adding the speeds and also mishandling the mass or time.
optionAnalysis.D: Incorrect. 90 N uses only the rebound speed (8 m/s) and ignores the incoming momentum.
optionAnalysis.E: Correct. Accounts for the reversal: |Δp| = 3.6 kg·m/s, so F = 3.6/0.020 = 180 N.

subtopic: Reversible adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas
learningObjective: Use the adiabatic relation T·V^(γ−1) = constant to find the final temperature of a monatomic ideal gas.
stem: A fixed quantity of an ideal monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) expands reversibly and adiabatically until its volume has doubled. If the initial absolute temperature of the gas is T, what is its final absolute temperature?
explanation: For a reversible adiabatic process, T·V^(γ−1) is constant, so T1·V1^(γ−1) = T2·V2^(γ−1). With γ = 5/3, the exponent γ − 1 = 2/3. Hence T2 = T1·(V1/V2)^(2/3) = T·(1/2)^(2/3) = T / 2^(2/3) = T / ∛4 (since 2^(2/3) = (2²)^(1/3) = ∛4 ≈ 1.59). The gas cools to about 0.63 T.

optionAnalysis.A: Incorrect. T/2 would follow from an isothermal-style or incorrect linear assumption, ignoring γ.
optionAnalysis.B: Incorrect. 2T/3 has no basis in the adiabatic relation.
optionAnalysis.C: Incorrect. T/4 uses an exponent of 2 instead of 2/3.
optionAnalysis.E: Incorrect. T·∛2 makes the gas warm on expansion, which is impossible for an adiabatic expansion doing work.

subtopic: banked curve with friction, maximum speed
learningObjective: Combine banking angle and friction to find the maximum safe speed on a curved road, integrating Newton's second law in two directions.
stem: A curved road of radius 50 m is banked at an angle such that tan(theta) = 0.75. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is 0.25. Take g = 10 m/s^2. What is the maximum speed at which a car can round the curve without sliding outward?
explanation: For the maximum speed, friction acts down the slope (preventing outward slide). Resolving along horizontal and vertical: v_max^2 = rg(tan theta + mu)/(1 - mu tan theta) = 50*10*(0.75 + 0.25)/(1 - 0.25*0.75) = 500*(1.00)/(1 - 0.1875) = 500/0.8125 = 615.4, so v_max = 24.8 m/s ≈ 25 m/s. The key traps are the sign of mu (down-slope at maximum speed) and the denominator term (1 - mu tan theta).

optionAnalysis.A: 22 m/s ignores the denominator correction, using v^2 = rg(tan theta + mu) = 500 → 22.4 m/s.
optionAnalysis.B: 15 m/s comes from subtracting mu from tan theta (friction up-slope, the minimum-speed case) instead of adding.
optionAnalysis.C: 19 m/s uses the frictionless banking speed v^2 = rg tan theta = 375 → 19.4 m/s, ignoring friction.
optionAnalysis.D: 30 m/s reverses the friction sign, using (tan theta + mu)/(1 + ... ) errors or adding rather than the correct combination, overestimating.
optionAnalysis.E: CORRECT: v_max^2 = rg(tan theta + mu)/(1 - mu tan theta) = 500(1.00)/(0.8125) ≈ 615, v ≈ 25 m/s.

subtopic: two-dimensional collision and kinetic-energy loss
learningObjective: Apply conservation of momentum to a perpendicular collision and compute the fraction of kinetic energy lost.
stem: On a frictionless horizontal surface, a 3.0 kg puck moving east at 4.0 m/s strikes a 1.0 kg puck moving north at 6.0 m/s. The two pucks stick together after impact. What fraction of the total initial kinetic energy is lost in the collision?
explanation: Momentum is conserved in the collision. Before impact: p_x = (3.0)(4.0) = 12 kg·m/s (east), p_y = (1.0)(6.0) = 6.0 kg·m/s (north). The 4.0 kg combined mass moves with momentum p = √(12² + 6²) = √180 ≈ 13.4 kg·m/s, so v = 13.4/4.0 ≈ 3.35 m/s. Initial KE = ½(3.0)(4.0²) + ½(1.0)(6.0²) = 24 + 18 = 42 J. Final KE = ½(4.0)(3.35²) ≈ 22.5 J. Fraction of KE lost = (42 − 22.5)/42 ≈ 0.46, i.e. about 0.45.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong: 0.33 does not follow from a correct momentum-and-energy calculation.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong: 0.55 is close to the fraction of KE RETAINED (22.5/42 ≈ 0.54), i.e. the complement of the answer — a classic retained-vs-lost slip.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong: 0.25 typically comes from adding the momentum components as scalars (12 + 6 = 18) instead of using the Pythagorean resultant.
optionAnalysis.E: Wrong: 0.70 overestimates the loss, e.g. by assuming one puck is brought to rest.

subtopic: buoyancy combined with gas law under submersion
learningObjective: Integrate hydrostatic pressure, the ideal gas law and Archimedes' principle to determine the buoyant force on a compressible bubble at depth.
stem: A small air bubble is released at the bottom of a fresh-water lake where the absolute pressure is 3.0 atm and rises to a depth where the absolute pressure is 1.5 atm. Temperature is constant. If the buoyant force on the bubble at the deeper point is F, what is the buoyant force at the shallower point? (The bubble remains fully submerged and behaves as an ideal gas.)
explanation: Buoyant force equals the weight of water displaced, F_b = rho_water * g * V_bubble, so F_b is proportional to the bubble volume V. At constant temperature Boyle's law gives P*V = constant, so V is inversely proportional to absolute pressure. Going from 3.0 atm to 1.5 atm halves the pressure, doubling the volume, hence doubling the buoyant force. F_shallow = 2F. The water density is essentially constant, so the entire change comes from the gas expansion.

optionAnalysis.A: CORRECT: V ∝ 1/P (Boyle), pressure halves so V doubles, and F_b ∝ V, giving 2F.
optionAnalysis.B: 4F squares the pressure ratio, treating volume as inversely proportional to P^2.
